planets.britain: Britain declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, two days after the German invasion of Poland, and Winston Churchill became Prime Minister in May 1940. After the fall of France more than 338,000 Allied troops were evacuated from Dunkirk, and in the summer and autumn of 1940 the Royal Air Force defeated the Luftwaffe's bid for air superiority in the Battle of Britain, forcing Hitler to put off his planned invasion. German night bombing of London and other cities, the Blitz, lasted until May 1941. Britain was the base for the cross-Channel invasion of Normandy on 6 June 1944.
planets.ireland: Ireland, a self-governing state led by Eamon de Valera, stayed neutral throughout the war. A state of emergency proclaimed on 2 September 1939 gave the government sweeping powers of censorship, internment and economic control, a period known in Ireland as the Emergency. Britain had handed back the Treaty Ports of Berehaven, Cobh and Lough Swilly in 1938, so the Royal Navy fought the Battle of the Atlantic without them. German bombs killed civilians on Dublin's North Strand on 31 May 1941. Northern Ireland, part of the United Kingdom, was at war, and Belfast was heavily bombed in April 1941.
planets.france: France declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939 and was overrun in the Battle of France that began on 10 May 1940; an armistice followed on 22 June. Germany occupied the north and the Atlantic coast, while Marshal Philippe Petain's collaborationist regime at Vichy governed the south and the colonies; at least 72,500 Jews deported from France were killed in the Nazi camps. After the Allied landings in North Africa in November 1942, Germany and Italy occupied the whole country. The Normandy landings of 6 June 1944 began the liberation, and Paris was freed on 25 August 1944.
planets.belgium: Neutral Belgium was invaded by Germany on 10 May 1940, and after 18 days of fighting King Leopold III surrendered the army on 28 May without consulting his government, which carried on the war from London. The Belgian Congo stayed loyal to that government and gave the Allies significant resources. Under German military rule nearly 25,000 of Belgium's Jews were killed. Most of the country was liberated in September and October 1944, and in December 1944 Germany struck back through the Belgian Ardennes in the Battle of the Bulge.
planets.netherlands: The neutral Netherlands was invaded by Germany on 10 May 1940; the Dutch forces surrendered on 15 May, the day after the bombing of Rotterdam, and the government and royal family went into exile in London. About 70 per cent of the country's Jews were killed, the highest proportion in Western Europe. The south was liberated in the second half of 1944, but after the failure of Operation Market Garden the west endured the Hunger Winter of 1944 to 1945, in which about 20,000 people died. The occupation lasted until the German surrender in May 1945.
planets.switzerland: Switzerland stayed neutral throughout the war, mobilising its army under General Henri Guisan in September 1939 and planning to withdraw into a fortified National Redoubt in the Alps if invaded. From 1942 it was completely surrounded by Axis-held territory. It controlled the rail tunnels through the Alps between Germany and Italy, exported machine tools, watches and jewel bearings, and bought large amounts of German gold, some of it plundered from occupied countries. It sheltered some 300,000 refugees and was a centre of diplomacy and espionage, although between 10,000 and 24,000 Jewish refugees were refused entry.
planets.germany: Germany, ruled by Adolf Hitler's Nazi dictatorship since 1933, began the war in Europe by invading Poland on 1 September 1939. By 1940 it had conquered most of the continent, and its racial policies culminated in the Holocaust, the murder of around six million Jews, alongside millions of other civilians and prisoners of war. The Ruhr, the main centre of its heavy industry, and its cities suffered a growing Allied bombing campaign. Invaded from east and west, Germany lost Berlin to the Red Army, and its armed forces surrendered unconditionally on 8 May 1945.
planets.austria: Austria had been annexed by Germany in the Anschluss of March 1938 and fought the war as part of the German Reich; its Jews were driven out of public life within months. The Mauthausen concentration camp near Linz, opened in August 1938, grew into a network of nearly 100 subcamps in Austria and southern Germany. In November 1943 the Allies declared the annexation null and void and promised a free Austria. Soviet forces took Vienna on 13 April 1945, and on 27 April a provisional government under Karl Renner declared the country independent of Germany.
planets.czechoslovakia: Czechoslovakia lost the Sudetenland to Germany under the Munich Agreement of 1938, and in March 1939 Germany occupied Bohemia and Moravia as a protectorate while Slovakia became a separate client state of Germany. President Edvard Benes led a government in exile in London. Germany took over the country's arms industry, notably the Skoda Works at Plzen. Czechoslovak soldiers trained in Britain assassinated the acting Reich Protector, Reinhard Heydrich, in 1942, and the Germans answered with reprisals including the Lidice massacre. Between 294,000 and 320,000 citizens were murdered during the occupation, most of them Jews.
planets.hungary: The Kingdom of Hungary, ruled by Regent Miklos Horthy, regained territory from its neighbours with Axis backing and joined the Axis on 20 November 1940. Its troops took part in the invasions of Yugoslavia and the Soviet Union, and its Second Army was crushed on the Don early in 1943. German troops occupied Hungary on 19 March 1944, and within about eight weeks some 437,000 Jews were deported to Auschwitz, where almost all were murdered. After Horthy's armistice attempt in October 1944 the Arrow Cross took power, and Budapest fell to the Red Army in February 1945.
planets.norway: Neutral Norway was invaded by Germany on 9 April 1940, largely to secure the port of Narvik, through which Swedish iron ore was shipped to Germany. Norwegian and Allied forces fought on until 10 June 1940, and King Haakon VII and the government continued the war from London. Germany ruled through Reich Commissioner Josef Terboven, with the collaborator Vidkun Quisling installed as head of a puppet government in 1942. Norwegian commandos and Allied bombers attacked the Vemork plant, the world's first to mass-produce heavy water, to hinder German nuclear weapons research. German rule ended in May 1945.
planets.sweden: Sweden kept its official neutrality throughout the war, one of the few European states to do so. German industry depended heavily on Swedish iron ore, which was sold to Germany throughout the war, and in 1941 Sweden let a German division cross by rail from Norway to Finland; German soldiers on leave passed through until 1943. Later it leaned towards the Allies, sharing military intelligence, training Danish and Norwegian refugee soldiers and letting the Allies use its airbases in 1944 and 1945. It gave asylum to almost all of Denmark's Jews in October 1943.
planets.denmark: Neutral Denmark was invaded by Germany on 9 April 1940, and its government surrendered within six hours. Its king, parliament and police stayed in place under a policy of cooperation, while Germany made use of its airfields and ports at the entrance to the Baltic and of its farm produce. As resistance grew, the government refused further German demands, and on 29 August 1943 Germany imposed martial law and direct military rule. In October 1943 the resistance and ordinary Danes ferried some 7,500 of the country's 8,000 Jews to safety in Sweden. German rule ended on 5 May 1945.
planets.finland: Finland, an independent republic, was invaded by the Soviet Union on 30 November 1939 and held out in the Winter War until the Moscow Peace Treaty of 13 March 1940, which cost it 9 per cent of its territory. It joined the German attack on the Soviet Union in June 1941, the Continuation War, regained its lost land and helped besiege Leningrad from the north. After Soviet offensives in 1944 it signed the Moscow Armistice on 19 September 1944, ceding Petsamo, and then fought the Lapland War to expel German troops from its north.
planets.spain: Spain, ruled by General Francisco Franco after his victory in the Civil War, was officially neutral, though it declared itself non-belligerent after the fall of France. Franco met Hitler at Hendaye on 23 October 1940 but did not join the Axis, partly because Spain depended on American and British imports. He sent the volunteer Blue Division to fight the Soviet Union, let U-boats refuel in Spanish ports and sold tungsten to Germany. As the war turned, Spain withdrew the Blue Division under Allied pressure in October 1943, and an American oil embargo in 1944 forced it to curb tungsten exports.
planets.portugal: Portugal, ruled by Antonio de Oliveira Salazar's authoritarian Estado Novo, kept its centuries-old treaty ties with Britain but remained neutral. As Germany overran Europe, neutral Portugal became one of the last escape routes from the continent. Portugal and Spain became Germany's main sources of wolfram, or tungsten, vital for munitions, until Allied pressure led Salazar to embargo all wolfram exports on 5 June 1944. In August 1943 Portugal leased bases in the Azores to Britain, and in 1944 it allowed the United States to use them as well.
planets.gibraltar: Gibraltar, a British colony and fortress since the early eighteenth century, commanded almost all shipping between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Most of its civilians were evacuated in 1940 to make room for the garrison, and miles of tunnels were dug inside the Rock. The Royal Navy's Force H, based there, escorted convoys to besieged Malta. Italian frogmen and human torpedoes attacked the harbour, and Germany planned to seize the Rock in Operation Felix, which was never carried out. General Eisenhower set up his headquarters there to plan Operation Torch, the Allied invasion of French North Africa in November 1942.
planets.italy: The Kingdom of Italy, under Benito Mussolini's Fascist dictatorship, entered the war on Germany's side on 10 June 1940. Defeats in Greece and North Africa left it reliant on German help, and it lost its East African colonies in 1941. After the Allied landings in Sicily, Mussolini was dismissed on 25 July 1943 and Italy signed an armistice in September; Germany then occupied the north and centre and installed Mussolini as head of the Italian Social Republic. Allied armies fought slowly up the peninsula, taking Rome on 4 June 1944; hostilities in Italy ended on 2 May 1945.
planets.sicily: Sicily, the largest island in the Mediterranean and a region of the Kingdom of Italy, became the Allies' next objective after the Axis defeat in Tunisia. American, British and Canadian forces landed on its southern and south-eastern coasts on the night of 9 to 10 July 1943, in the campaign codenamed Operation Husky. Six weeks of fighting against the Italian 6th Army and German troops ended on 17 August, although many Germans and Italians escaped across the Strait of Messina. The invasion opened the Mediterranean to Allied merchant ships and led to the fall of Mussolini.
planets.sardinia: Sardinia, the second-largest Mediterranean island and a region of the Kingdom of Italy, was an important air and naval base; bombers flying from it attacked Gibraltar. Its coal mines around Carbonia, a new town founded in 1938, served Fascist Italy's drive for self-sufficiency. In 1943 the British deception Operation Mincemeat led the Germans to expect landings in Sardinia and Greece rather than Sicily, and Allied bombers struck its airfields and the port of Cagliari. After the Italian armistice of September 1943, the German garrison withdrew to Corsica without fighting under an agreement with the island's Italian commander.
planets.yugoslavia: The Kingdom of Yugoslavia joined the Tripartite Pact on 25 March 1941, but a coup in Belgrade overthrew the government two days later, and Germany invaded on 6 April; the army surrendered on 17 April. The country was partitioned among Germany, Italy, Hungary, Bulgaria and the new Independent State of Croatia, whose Ustase regime waged genocide against Serbs, Jews and Roma. Josip Broz Tito's communist Partisans and the royalist Chetniks fought the occupiers and each other. With Soviet help the Partisans took Belgrade on 20 October 1944. Around one million Yugoslavs died in the war, about half of them civilians.
planets.greece: The Kingdom of Greece rejected an Italian ultimatum on 28 October 1940 and drove the invading Italian army back into Albania. Germany invaded on 6 April 1941, overrunning the mainland despite British, Australian and New Zealand reinforcements, and the government went into exile. Greece was divided into German, Italian and Bulgarian occupation zones; plunder and blockade caused a famine in which some 300,000 people died, 40,000 of them in Athens, and most of Greece's Jews were deported to Auschwitz and Treblinka. German and Bulgarian forces withdrew from the mainland in October 1944.
planets.romania: The Kingdom of Romania lost Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina to the Soviet Union and Northern Transylvania to Hungary in 1940, after which Marshal Ion Antonescu took power and joined the Axis on 23 November 1940. Its oil, refined around Ploiesti, supplied Germany; American bombers struck the refineries in a costly raid on 1 August 1943. Romania sent more troops against the Soviet Union than all Germany's other allies combined, and its forces were responsible for the massacre of some 260,000 Jews. On 23 August 1944, as the Red Army broke through, King Michael deposed Antonescu and Romania changed sides.
planets.bulgaria: The Kingdom of Bulgaria under Tsar Boris III regained Southern Dobruja in 1940 and joined the Axis on 1 March 1941, and German troops invaded Yugoslavia and Greece from its soil. With German consent it occupied Yugoslav Macedonia and Greek Western Thrace, and declared war on Britain and the United States in December 1941, but not on the Soviet Union. It sent 11,343 Jews from the occupied lands to their deaths, while the 48,000 Jews of Bulgaria itself survived. The Red Army entered on 8 September 1944, and Bulgaria declared war on Germany the next day.
planets.crete: The Greek island of Crete was held by British Commonwealth and Greek troops when mainland Greece fell in April 1941. On 20 May 1941 Germany launched the first mainly airborne invasion in history; the loss of Maleme airfield let German reinforcements land, and by 1 June the island had fallen, with more than half its defenders evacuated by the Royal Navy. Cretan civilians fought the invaders and suffered mass reprisals, including the destruction of Kandanos. German garrisons held the island until they surrendered after the war in Europe ended in 1945.
planets.poland: The Republic of Poland was invaded by Germany on 1 September 1939 and by the Soviet Union on 17 September, and was divided between them by 6 October. Its government carried on the war in exile in London. Occupied Poland became the centre of the Holocaust: over three million Polish Jews were murdered, chiefly at the Chelmno, Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz extermination camps, and around six million Polish citizens died in all. The Home Army rose in Warsaw on 1 August 1944 as the Red Army approached, but the uprising was crushed after 63 days and the city destroyed.
planets.baltic_states: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, three independent republics, were assigned to the Soviet sphere by the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, occupied by the Soviet Union in June 1940 and annexed that August, an annexation most Western countries refused to recognise; Soviet mass deportations followed in June 1941. Germany overran the region that summer and ruled it as part of the Reichskommissariat Ostland, and more than 95 per cent of Lithuania's Jews were murdered in the Holocaust. The Red Army retook most of the Baltic states in 1944, while German forces held out in the Courland Pocket until May 1945.
planets.belarus: Belarus, the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic, had been enlarged by Poland's eastern lands after the Soviet invasion of 1939, and Germany overran it by the end of August 1941. Under German occupation more than two million people were killed, about a quarter of the population, including 500,000 to 550,000 Jews, and more than 600 villages such as Khatyn were wiped out with all their inhabitants. Soviet partisans struck German supply lines from the forests and swamps. The Red Army's Operation Bagration, launched on 22 June 1944, freed Minsk on 4 July and the whole republic by the end of August.
planets.ukraine: Ukraine, the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, whose farmland and Donbas industrial region Germany meant to exploit, was invaded in June 1941; the battle for Kiev, which fell on 19 September, trapped over 450,000 Soviet troops in the largest encirclement in history. Under the Reichskommissariat Ukraine, Germany plundered the country and pursued genocide: between 900,000 and 1.6 million Jews were murdered, 33,771 of them at Babi Yar on 29 and 30 September 1941, and millions of other civilians died. The Red Army liberated most of Ukraine in 1943 and 1944.
planets.russia: Russia, the heart of Joseph Stalin's Soviet Union and home of its capital, Moscow, bore the brunt of Germany's invasion of 22 June 1941. The German advance on Moscow was halted and driven back between October 1941 and January 1942, while Leningrad endured an 872-day siege that cost an estimated 1.5 million lives. At Stalingrad on the Volga the German 6th Army was destroyed, surrendering on 2 February 1943, and the German offensive at Kursk in July 1943 was defeated. From then on the Red Army held the initiative until it reached Berlin.
planets.caucasus: The Caucasus, comprising the Soviet republics of Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan and the North Caucasus region of Soviet Russia, held the oil fields of Baku, Grozny and Maikop, the goal of Germany's summer offensive of 1942. After taking Rostov-on-Don in July, German forces captured the demolished Maikop oilfields and reached Ordzhonikidze in November, but never reached Baku; that winter, Soviet offensives around Stalingrad forced them to withdraw. In February 1944 the Soviet government deported the entire Chechen and Ingush peoples of the North Caucasus to Central Asia, and at least a quarter of the 496,000 deportees died.
planets.urals: The Urals, the mountain range dividing European Russia from Siberia, were an industrial region of Soviet Russia far beyond the reach of German armies and bombers. In 1941 hundreds of factories were evacuated from European Russia and Ukraine to the eastern foothills of the Urals, where Stalin's industrial drive had already built the Magnitogorsk steelworks. Giant tank plants grew at Uralmash in Sverdlovsk, Uralvagonzavod in Nizhny Tagil and Chelyabinsk, nicknamed Tankograd, which absorbed most of Leningrad's Kirov Plant and built 18,000 tanks during the war. These evacuations helped Soviet war production rise substantially from late 1941 to early 1943.
planets.kazakhstan: Kazakhstan, as the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic, lay deep in the Soviet interior, far from the front. When Germany invaded, many large factories were moved there, and the republic developed oil wells, mines, steel plants and refineries. Many Kazakhs served with distinction: the 316th Rifle Division, raised at Alma-Ata in July 1941 from mostly Kazakh and Kyrgyz reservists, fought before Moscow and was made a Guards division. The republic also received whole peoples deported by Stalin, among them Volga Germans and, from February 1944, Chechens and Ingush, at least a quarter of whom died.
planets.siberia: Siberia, stretching from the Urals to the Pacific, was part of Soviet Russia, far beyond the reach of German armies. Until June 1941 its Trans-Siberian Railway was Germany's only reliable trade link with Japan, carrying rubber westwards; after the invasion it helped move Soviet industry east. Told by the spy Richard Sorge that Japan would not attack, Stalin transferred over 18 divisions, 1,700 tanks and 1,500 aircraft from Siberia and the Far East to defend Moscow. The Pacific route through Vladivostok became the safest path for American aid, and in 1945 the railway carried forces for the attack on Japan.
planets.morocco: Morocco was a French protectorate under Sultan Muhammad V, with a smaller Spanish protectorate in the north, and after France's defeat in 1940 it came under the Vichy regime. On 8 November 1942 American troops landed on its Atlantic coast in Operation Torch and took Casablanca, the principal French Atlantic naval base, after a short siege. In January 1943 Roosevelt and Churchill met at Casablanca to plan Allied strategy, with the Sultan among those attending. Moroccan troops, notably the goumiers, then fought for the Allies, and in January 1944 the Istiqlal Party issued a manifesto demanding independence.
planets.algeria: Algeria, ruled by France since 1830 and governed as French departments, came under Vichy rule in 1940; on 3 July 1940 the Royal Navy attacked the French fleet at Mers El Kebir near Oran, killing more than 1,200 men. On 8 November 1942 Allied forces landed at Oran and Algiers in Operation Torch, and from 1943 Algiers served as the capital of Free France. Algerian troops fought for France in Italy and southern France. After a victory parade at Setif on 8 May 1945 turned violent, French forces and settlers killed thousands of Algerians; historians estimate 3,000 to 30,000.
planets.tunisia: Tunisia, a French protectorate ruled in name by its bey, was governed after 1940 by Vichy France's Resident-General, Admiral Jean-Pierre Esteva. When the Allies landed in Algeria in November 1942, German and Italian troops poured in, and for six months Tunisia was a battlefield, scene of the Axis victory at Kasserine Pass. The Allies entered Tunis on 7 May 1943, and the Axis armies surrendered days later, leaving over 260,000 prisoners. The Free French then deposed Moncef Bey, accusing him of collaboration, and Tunisia became the springboard for the invasion of Sicily.
planets.libya: Libya, an Italian colony formed from Tripolitania and Cyrenaica, was the main battleground of the desert war. The exiled Senussi leader Idris backed Britain, and a Libyan Arab Force of volunteers fought beside the British, including at Tobruk. A British counter-offensive against Italy's invasion of Egypt destroyed the Italian 10th Army early in 1941, before Rommel's Afrika Korps drove the British back; Tobruk, held mainly by Australians, withstood a 231-day siege in 1941 but fell in June 1942. After El Alamein the British 8th Army took Tripoli on 23 January 1943, and Libya passed under British and French administration.
planets.egypt: The Kingdom of Egypt under King Farouk was formally independent, but the 1936 treaty with Britain allowed British troops to reoccupy the country in wartime, and the Suez Canal made it vital to Britain. Egypt broke off relations with Germany and Italy but stayed neutral, even when Italy invaded in 1940. In February 1942 British tanks surrounded Abdeen Palace to force Farouk to appoint a Wafd government. Rommel was halted at El Alamein in July 1942, and Montgomery's victory there in November drove the Axis out of Egypt. It declared war on the Axis only on 24 February 1945.
planets.malta: Malta, a British colony and the only Allied base between Gibraltar and Alexandria, lay across the Axis supply routes to North Africa. From June 1940 to November 1942 Italian and German aircraft besieged it with some 3,000 bombing raids, while convoys such as Operation Pedestal in August 1942 fought through to keep it supplied. Aircraft, ships and submarines from Malta attacked Axis convoys bound for Libya. King George VI awarded the island the George Cross on 15 April 1942, and Malta later served as a base for the invasion of Sicily.
planets.turkey: The Republic of Turkey signed a mutual aid pact with Britain and France in 1939 but stayed neutral, fearing a Soviet attack on Istanbul or its Caucasus border, and in June 1941 it also signed a treaty of friendship with Germany. Its chromite, used for stainless steel, was sought by both sides, the Allies buying it mainly to keep it from Germany. Turkey halted sales to Germany in April 1944 and broke off relations that August. It declared war on the Axis in February 1945, when the Allies made full belligerency a condition for joining the new United Nations.
planets.syria: Syria and Lebanon, held by France under League of Nations mandates, came under Vichy French control after the fall of France. When Vichy let German aircraft use Syrian airfields to support the anti-British regime in Iraq in May 1941, British Empire and Free French forces invaded in June. The Vichy French fought hard but sought an armistice as Australian troops neared Beirut, and it was signed at Acre on 14 July 1941. Both territories stayed under Allied occupation for the rest of the war; Lebanon was declared independent on 22 November 1943, and Syria proclaimed its independence in 1944.
planets.palestine: Palestine was governed by Britain under a League of Nations mandate and served as a British staging area and a source of troops. The White Paper of 1939 severely restricted Jewish immigration and land purchase, yet the Jewish community backed the war against Germany: about 30,000 Jews from Palestine served in the British forces, and a Jewish Brigade formed in 1944 fought in Italy. Up to 12,000 Palestinian Arabs also volunteered. From July 1940 Italian aircraft bombed Haifa, with its port and oil refineries, and Tel Aviv, and in 1942 the German advance into Egypt raised fears of invasion.
planets.iraq: The Kingdom of Iraq, nominally independent since 1932 but bound by treaty to allow British bases, mattered to Britain for its oil and as a land bridge between Egypt and India. In April 1941 the Golden Square coup brought the pro-Axis Rashid Ali al-Gaylani to power, and German aircraft flew in through Syria. British and Indian forces defeated his regime in the Anglo-Iraqi War of May 1941 and restored the pro-British Regent. In the Farhud pogrom in Baghdad on 1 and 2 June 1941, more than 180 Jews were killed. Iraq declared war on the Axis in 1943.
planets.persia: Persia, or Iran, was a neutral monarchy under Reza Shah Pahlavi, with British-owned oil installations and the new Trans-Iranian Railway. In August 1941 British and Soviet forces invaded to secure the oil and a supply route to the Soviet Union, and on 16 September Reza Shah was forced to abdicate in favour of his son, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi. The country became the Persian Corridor, through which 45 per cent of American Lend-Lease aid to the Soviet Union, by tonnage, passed. Iran declared war on Germany in September 1943, and Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill met at Tehran that November.
planets.iceland: Iceland, a sovereign kingdom in personal union with Denmark, declared its neutrality and stayed officially neutral throughout the war. After Germany occupied Denmark, British forces landed at Reykjavik on 10 May 1940 and occupied the island without resistance to forestall a German move, and on 7 July 1941 the still-neutral United States took over its defence. Air bases such as Keflavik supported the fight against U-boats in the Battle of the Atlantic, and the occupation brought an economic boom. On 17 June 1944 Iceland ended its union with Denmark and became a republic.
planets.greenland: Greenland, a Danish colony, was left on its own when Germany occupied Denmark in April 1940, and its two sheriffs declared it self-governing. Its most strategic asset was the mine at Ivigtut, which produced cryolite, used in smelting aluminium. On 9 April 1941 the Danish envoy in Washington, Henrik Kauffmann, signed a treaty letting the United States defend Greenland, and American air and naval bases, codenamed Bluie, and weather stations followed. From August 1942 the Germans set up clandestine weather stations on the east coast, and a small Northeast Greenland Sledge Patrol hunted for them.
planets.azores: The Azores, Portuguese islands in the mid-Atlantic, were coveted by both sides, and Portugal sent some 28,000 troops to guard them and its neutrality. Under an agreement signed with Britain in August 1943, the Royal Air Force arrived on Terceira in October and flew anti-submarine patrols from Lajes Field, sinking its first U-boat in November. American transport aircraft followed from December 1943, and by the end of June 1944 more than 1,900 had passed through, nearly halving flying times on the Atlantic ferry route.
planets.newfoundland: Newfoundland, a British dominion governed directly by Britain through an appointed Commission of Government, was at war from September 1939, and Canada took responsibility for its defence after the fall of France. Under the Destroyers for Bases deal the United States built bases on the island, among them Naval Station Argentia, where Churchill and Roosevelt issued the Atlantic Charter on 14 August 1941. Some 15,000 Newfoundlanders served and about 900 died. U-boats sank ore carriers off Bell Island in 1942 and, on 14 October, the ferry SS Caribou, with the loss of 137 lives.
planets.united_states: The United States stayed neutral when war broke out in Europe, but from March 1941 its Lend-Lease programme supplied Britain and later the Soviet Union, China and other Allies with some $50 billion of food, oil and war materiel. Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941 brought it into the war, and Germany and Italy declared war on it on 11 December. American forces fought in North Africa, Italy and Western Europe and across the Pacific. The Manhattan Project built the first atomic bombs, which were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6 and 9 August 1945.
planets.canada: Canada, a self-governing dominion of the British Empire, declared war on Germany on 10 September 1939, a week after Britain. About 1.1 million Canadians served, and some 42,000 were killed. Some 130,000 Allied pilots trained in Canada under the British Commonwealth Air Training Plan, its merchant navy made over 25,000 Atlantic voyages, and by 1945 it had the world's third-largest navy. Canadians suffered heavy losses in the Dieppe Raid of August 1942, fought through Sicily and Italy, and landed on Juno Beach in Normandy on 6 June 1944. Canada itself came under attack in the Battle of the St. Lawrence.
planets.alaska: Alaska, a United States territory, gained new strategic importance in the war. After bombing the naval base at Dutch Harbor, Japan occupied the Aleutian islands of Attu and Kiska in June 1942, the only campaign of the war fought on North American soil; American forces retook Attu in May 1943, and an American-Canadian force found Kiska abandoned in August. Over 880 Unangax, or Aleuts, were evacuated to camps in the Alaska Panhandle, where about one in ten died. The Alaska Highway, completed through Canada in October 1942, linked the airfields that ferried Lend-Lease aircraft to the Soviet Union.
planets.mexico: Mexico, under President Manuel Avila Camacho, entered the war after German U-boats sank the tankers Potrero del Llano and Faja de Oro in May 1942, declaring war on the Axis on 22 May. It supplied the United States with more strategic raw materials than any other country, and under the Bracero program tens of thousands of Mexican workers were hired for American farms. As many as 250,000 Mexicans living in the United States served in its armed forces, and Mexico's own 201st Fighter Squadron flew in combat over Luzon in the Philippines in 1945.
planets.panama: The Republic of Panama was crossed by the Panama Canal, whose surrounding Canal Zone was United States territory. The canal let American warships and troops move quickly between the Atlantic and the Pacific, and it was vital for sending new warships from eastern shipyards to fight Japan; the United States fortified its approaches extensively. President Arnulfo Arias, an outspoken nationalist, was deposed by the National Police in October 1941, to the evident relief of American officials. Under a 1942 agreement Panama granted the United States further bases, including the airfield at Rio Hato.
planets.japan: The Empire of Japan, under Emperor Hirohito and a military-dominated government, had been at war with China since 1937 and joined Germany and Italy in the Tripartite Pact in 1940. Facing an American oil embargo, it attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941 and then overran Southeast Asia and much of the Pacific. After defeats at Midway and Guadalcanal it was driven back, and American B-29s firebombed its cities, killing some 100,000 people in Tokyo on one night in March 1945. After the atomic bombings and Soviet entry into the war, Japan announced its surrender on 15 August 1945.
planets.korea: Korea had been ruled by Japan as a colony since 1910, governed from Seoul by a Japanese Governor-General. Japan intensified forced assimilation, pressing Koreans to take Japanese names, and mobilised the peninsula for war: hundreds of thousands of Korean men were sent to Japan as forced labourers, Koreans were conscripted into the army from 1944, and many women and girls were forced into sexual slavery as so-called comfort women. The Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea, in exile in Chongqing, declared war on Japan in December 1941. Japan's surrender in August 1945 ended its rule.
planets.manchuria: Manchuria, in north-east China, was seized by Japan after the Mukden incident of 1931 and made the puppet state of Manchukuo, with the last Qing emperor, Puyi, as its nominal ruler. Japan built up heavy industry there with the slave labour of local people, settled over a million Japanese colonists and used it as the main launching ground for its invasion of China. In 1939 Soviet and Mongolian forces under Georgy Zhukov defeated the Japanese at Khalkhin Gol on the Mongolian border. At Harbin, Unit 731 carried out lethal human experiments. The Soviet invasion of 8 August 1945 overran Manchukuo.
planets.china: The Republic of China, under Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government, had been resisting a full-scale Japanese invasion since July 1937; that December Japanese troops captured the capital, Nanjing, and carried out the Nanjing Massacre. The government moved to Chongqing, and by 1939 the war had reached a stalemate, with Mao Zedong's Communists waging guerrilla war from Shaanxi and Japanese scorched-earth campaigns killing millions of civilians. After Pearl Harbor the United States became China's main backer; supplies came along the Burma Road and, once that was cut, by air over the Himalayas. Japan's Ichi-Go offensive of 1944 overran Henan and Changsha.
planets.formosa: Formosa, or Taiwan, had been a Japanese colony since China ceded it in 1895, governed from Taihoku by a Japanese Governor-General. From 1937 Japan pressed a campaign to Japanize its people and expanded its industry for war production; over 207,000 Taiwanese worked for the Japanese military. The island was a base for Japan's attack on the Philippines. In the Cairo Declaration of 1943 the Allies promised to return it to China. American carrier aircraft destroyed over 300 Japanese planes in the Formosa Air Battle of October 1944, and bombing killed an estimated 16,000 to 30,000 civilians.
planets.indochina: French Indochina, comprising Cochinchina, Annam, Tonkin, Cambodia and Laos, stayed loyal to Vichy France after 1940. Japan occupied the north in September 1940 to cut China's supply line from Haiphong and took over the whole territory in July 1941, later using it as a base for the invasion of Malaya. Ho Chi Minh revived the Viet Minh to fight the occupation. On 9 March 1945 Japan overthrew the French administration, and a famine in northern Vietnam from late 1944 killed between 400,000 and 2 million people. At the war's end the Viet Minh proclaimed Vietnam's independence.
planets.siam: Siam, or Thailand, an independent kingdom led by the military prime minister Plaek Phibunsongkhram, fought Vichy French Indochina for lost territory in 1940 and 1941. Japan invaded on 8 December 1941; after five hours Thailand agreed to an armistice and then a pact, let Japanese troops pass to invade Malaya and Burma, and on 25 January 1942 declared war on Britain and the United States. The Burma Railway was built from Thailand into Burma by forced labourers and prisoners of war. The pro-Allied Free Thai Movement resisted the Japanese and helped bring about Phibun's fall in 1944.
planets.burma: Burma, a British colony separated from India in 1937, carried supplies to China along the Burma Road, and cutting it helped motivate Japan's invasion in 1942. Japan held most of it by April 1942 and in August 1943 declared it independent as the State of Burma under Ba Maw. Forced labourers and Allied prisoners built the Burma Railway to supply the Japanese; more than 100,000 of them died. In August 1944 Aung San's nationalists formed the Anti-Fascist Organisation and turned to the British, whose forces retook Rangoon in May 1945. Between 170,000 and 250,000 civilians died under the occupation.
planets.malaya: Malaya, under British rule and producer of 40 per cent of the world's rubber and much of its tin, was invaded by Japan on 8 December 1941; two days later Japanese aircraft sank the warships Prince of Wales and Repulse. Japanese troops swept down the peninsula, and on 15 February 1942 Singapore, Britain's foremost base in South-East Asia, surrendered in the largest capitulation in British history. The Japanese then massacred many ethnic Chinese in the Sook Ching purge. Four northern Malay states were handed to Thailand, and the communist-led Malayan Peoples' Anti-Japanese Army resisted until Japan's surrender in 1945.
planets.philippines: The Commonwealth of the Philippines, a semi-independent American commonwealth due for independence in 1946, was attacked by Japan on 8 December 1941, hours after Pearl Harbor. American and Filipino forces under Douglas MacArthur held out on the Bataan Peninsula until 9 April 1942; thousands of prisoners died on the Bataan Death March that followed, and Corregidor fell on 6 May. Filipino guerrillas resisted throughout the occupation. MacArthur returned at Leyte in October 1944, as the Japanese navy was defeated at Leyte Gulf, and the battle for Manila in February and March 1945 killed at least 100,000 civilians.
planets.dutch_east_indies: The Dutch East Indies, the world's fourth-largest oil exporter, was a prime Japanese objective because Japan lacked oil of its own. Japan invaded on 10 January 1942, defeated an Allied fleet in the Battle of the Java Sea on 27 February, and received the Dutch surrender on 8 March. Under occupation millions of Indonesians were recruited as forced labourers, or romusha, and some four million people died of famine and forced labour, including 30,000 European civilian internees. Allied forces largely bypassed the islands, and on 17 August 1945 Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta proclaimed Indonesia's independence.
planets.india: British India was taken into the war by its Viceroy in September 1939 without consulting the Indian people. It raised over two and a half million soldiers, the largest army raised by voluntary enlistment, who fought in Africa, Europe and Asia, and it was the base for American operations in support of China. When Gandhi launched the Quit India movement in August 1942, almost the entire Congress leadership was imprisoned. The Bengal famine of 1943 killed an estimated 800,000 to 3.8 million people. In 1944 Japanese forces invaded north-east India and were defeated at Imphal and Kohima.
planets.ceylon: Ceylon, a British Crown colony with harbours at Colombo and Trincomalee, lay beside the shipping routes from South-East Asia to the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf, and became a front-line British base against Japan and an important source of rubber. On 5 April 1942 Japanese carrier aircraft attacked Colombo, hoping to destroy the British Eastern Fleet, but most of it had been dispersed and survived. In May 1942 Ceylonese gunners on the Cocos Islands mutinied, intending to hand the islands to Japan. From April 1944 Kandy was the headquarters of Lord Mountbatten's South East Asia Command.
planets.afghanistan: The Kingdom of Afghanistan, ruled by King Mohammad Zahir Shah with Mohammad Hashim Khan as prime minister, stayed neutral throughout the war and was never attacked. Despite British pressure it kept friendly relations with the Axis, hoping to curb British influence from India, and in 1940 its legation in Berlin asked whether a victorious Germany would give it the Pashtun lands between the Durand Line and the Indus. Its relations with Nazi Germany were severed after the Anglo-Soviet invasion of neighbouring Iran in 1941, and it remained non-aligned for the rest of the war.
planets.hawaii: Hawaii, a United States territory since 1898, was home to the United States Pacific Fleet, based at Pearl Harbor on Oahu since 1940. On 7 December 1941 Japanese carrier aircraft attacked the fleet without warning: all eight battleships present were damaged and four were sunk, and 2,403 Americans were killed. The attack brought the United States into the war. The islands were then placed under martial law until 1944, with a military governor controlling every aspect of civilian life.
planets.midway: Midway, a small American atoll about 1,300 miles north-west of Oahu, had held a naval air station since 1941 and was attacked four times between December 1941 and February 1942. In June 1942 Admiral Yamamoto moved to capture it and draw out the American carriers, but code breakers had revealed his plan. In the Battle of Midway, fought from 4 to 7 June 1942, American carrier and island-based aircraft sank all four Japanese fleet carriers present, a decisive defeat for the Japanese navy six months after Pearl Harbor. The atoll then served as a base for submarines patrolling Japanese waters.
planets.wake_island: Wake Island, a small American atoll in the central Pacific, was bombed on 8 December 1941, within hours of Pearl Harbor. Its garrison, with Marines playing a prominent role, beat off a first Japanese landing on 11 December, but a second assault forced its surrender on 23 December, and nearly 1,200 civilian contractors were captured along with the troops. Japan held the island for the rest of the war while American aircraft and warships raided it. After one such raid, on 7 October 1943, the Japanese commander had the 97 civilian prisoners still on the island executed.
planets.marshall_islands: The Marshall Islands, a former German possession, had been governed by Japan since the First World War under the League of Nations' South Seas Mandate and served as an important outpost of the Japanese navy. In Operation Flintlock, American forces landed on Majuro and Kwajalein on 31 January 1944; the capture of Kwajalein by 3 February was the first American break into the outer ring of Japan's Pacific defences, and on Roi-Namur only 51 of some 3,500 defenders survived. Eniwetok followed from 17 to 23 February, giving the Americans an airfield and harbour for the attack on the Marianas.
planets.marianas: The Marianas combined Saipan and Tinian, governed by Japan under the League of Nations' South Seas Mandate, with Guam, an American territory seized by Japan in December 1941. In Operation Forager, American forces landed on Saipan on 15 June 1944, provoking the Battle of the Philippine Sea, which effectively destroyed Japanese carrier air power; about 1,000 civilians took their own lives as resistance ended, and the loss brought down Prime Minister Tojo. Guam and Tinian were taken by 10 August. From the islands' airfields B-29s bombed Japan, and aircraft from Tinian carried out the atomic bombings of August 1945.
planets.gilbert_islands: The Gilbert Islands, part of the British colony of the Gilbert and Ellice Islands, were occupied by Japan from 10 December 1941, when troops landed unopposed on Makin; Ocean Island, with its phosphate mines, was taken in 1942. Using the Ellice Islands as a staging post, American forces struck back on 20 November 1943 in the first offensive of the Central Pacific drive. On Betio, a tiny island of Tarawa atoll, 4,500 well-prepared Japanese defenders fought almost to the last man, and nearly 6,400 Japanese, Koreans and Americans died in four days. Makin fell the same week.
planets.new_guinea: New Guinea was divided between the Australian-run Territories of New Guinea and Papua and a Dutch colony in the west. Japan invaded the Territory of New Guinea in January 1942, making Rabaul a major air and naval base, and in July landed in Papua to strike overland at Port Moresby along the Kokoda Track. Australian troops, helped by Papuan carriers, halted that advance, and their victory at Milne Bay in September 1942 was the first full-scale Japanese defeat on land. Allied forces, mostly Australian, fought on there until the war's end; disease and starvation killed more Japanese than combat.
planets.solomon_islands: The Solomon Islands, a British protectorate governed from Tulagi, were occupied by Japan in the first half of 1942 as it built bases to protect the flank of its offensive in New Guinea. On 7 August 1942 United States Marines landed on Guadalcanal and Tulagi in the first major Allied land offensive against Japan, seizing the airfield that became Henderson Field. Six months of land and naval battles followed until the Japanese evacuated Guadalcanal in February 1943, and fighting went on in New Georgia and Bougainville. Islander scouts and coastwatchers warned the Allies of Japanese attacks.
planets.australia: Australia entered the war on 3 September 1939 alongside Britain, and almost one million Australians served in its forces, first in North Africa and the Mediterranean and then against Japan. The country came under direct attack for the first time: 188 Japanese aircraft bombed Darwin on 19 February 1942, the first of more than 100 air raids, and midget submarines entered Sydney Harbour on 31 May 1942. From 1942 until early 1944 Australians made up most of the Allied strength in the South West Pacific. Of 21,467 Australians taken prisoner by the Japanese, only 14,000 survived.
planets.new_zealand: New Zealand declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939 alongside Britain, and on Japan after Pearl Harbor. Its army division fought in Greece, North Africa and Italy, and Lieutenant-General Bernard Freyberg commanded the defence of Crete in 1941. Many of its airmen served in the Royal Air Force, and its warships fought in the Battle of the River Plate in 1939. In the Pacific its navy, air force and army brigades fought in the Solomons alongside American forces. Though its home islands were never attacked, its military casualty rate per head was the highest in the Commonwealth after Britain's.
planets.fiji: Fiji, a British colony in the South Pacific, became an Allied training base and a major port for convoys between the United States and Australia, and an airstrip was built at Nadi. Many thousands of indigenous Fijians volunteered for the Fiji Infantry Regiment, which served with New Zealand and Australian units and fought in the Solomon Islands campaign; Corporal Sefanaia Sukanaivalu was posthumously awarded the Victoria Cross for his bravery on Bougainville. Most Indo-Fijians declined to enlist after their demand for equal treatment with Europeans was refused. Seaplanes launched from Japanese submarines flew over the islands in 1941 and 1942.
planets.brazil: Brazil, ruled by President Getulio Vargas, was neutral at first but broke off relations with Germany, Italy and Japan in January 1942 and let the United States build air bases on its soil; the base at Natal became the largest American air base outside American territory. After Axis submarines had sunk 36 Brazilian merchant ships, Brazil declared war on Germany and Italy on 22 August 1942. Its navy and air force fought in the Battle of the Atlantic, and its Expeditionary Force of about 25,900 men fought in Italy from September 1944, the only South American troops sent overseas.
planets.argentina: Argentina, a leading food exporter with strong trade ties to Britain, kept its long tradition of neutrality through most of the war despite mounting pressure from the United States. Its government was at first sympathetic to the Allies and aided Britain economically, but a military coup in 1943 brought to power officers accused of Axis sympathies, and Buenos Aires became a major centre of Axis espionage. Argentina broke off relations with the Axis on 26 January 1944 and declared war on 27 March 1945. Over 4,000 Argentine volunteers fought on the Allied side.
planets.chile: Chile, a republic with a large German community and close trade ties to Germany, declared its neutrality when war broke out in Europe; its own National Socialist movement had attempted a coup in 1938. Under growing American pressure the government later distanced itself from the Axis and dismissed pro-German officers. After a U-boat sank the Chilean ship Tolten off the United States coast and anti-German demonstrations followed, Chile broke off relations with the Axis on 20 January 1943. It strengthened its naval presence around Easter Island against a feared Japanese attack, and on 13 April 1945 declared war on Japan.
planets.venezuela: Venezuela, neutral at the outbreak of war under President Eleazar Lopez Contreras, was then the world's leading oil exporter, and in the early war years most of Britain's oil came from Venezuelan fields by way of the refineries on Dutch Curacao. It broke off relations with the Axis on 31 December 1941. On 16 February 1942 German U-boats attacked the refineries of Aruba and Curacao and the shallow tankers carrying crude from Lake Maracaibo, sinking the Venezuelan ship Monagas. Venezuela won a fifty-fifty share of oil profits and declared war on the Axis on 15 February 1945.
planets.west_africa: French West Africa, a federation of eight colonies including Senegal and the Ivory Coast, was governed from the port of Dakar. After the fall of France its authorities declared for Vichy, and in September 1940 an Allied attempt to win Dakar over to General de Gaulle's Free French failed. It remained under Vichy control until the Allied landings in North Africa in November 1942, after which its colonial troops strengthened the Free French. On 1 December 1944 French troops at Thiaroye killed between 35 and 300 repatriated West African soldiers protesting over unpaid wages.
planets.congo: The Belgian Congo, under Governor-General Pierre Ryckmans, stayed loyal to the Belgian government in exile in London and became a crucial source of income for it. Its Force Publique, with Belgian officers, fought the Italians in Italian East Africa and cut off the Italian forces that surrendered at Saio on 3 July 1941. It supplied the Allies with gold, rubber after Malaya fell, and uranium from the Shinkolobwe mine, used in the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Heavy wartime demands on its people provoked strikes and a mutiny at Luluabourg in 1944.
planets.east_africa: In East Africa, Italy had conquered Ethiopia in 1936 and joined it with Eritrea and Italian Somaliland as Italian East Africa. Emperor Haile Selassie went into exile in England, while Ethiopian patriots, the Arbegnoch, kept up a guerrilla war. After Italy entered the war, British Empire forces, joined by Belgian Congolese, Free French and Ethiopian troops, invaded from Sudan and Kenya. Haile Selassie returned to Ethiopia on 20 January 1941 with Orde Wingate's Gideon Force, Addis Ababa fell on 6 April, and he re-entered it on 5 May 1941. The last Italian forces surrendered at Gondar in November 1941.
planets.south_africa: The Union of South Africa, a self-governing dominion, was divided over the war: when Prime Minister Hertzog sought neutrality, his party deposed him, and his successor Jan Smuts declared war on Germany on 6 September 1939. Its control of the sea route around the Cape of Good Hope made it strategically vital. South African divisions fought in East Africa, North Africa and Italy, and most of the 2nd Division was captured when Tobruk fell on 21 June 1942. South Africa trained 33,347 aircrew for Allied air forces, while Smuts jailed leaders of the pro-Nazi Ossewabrandwag, including John Vorster.
planets.madagascar: Madagascar, a French colony, sided with Vichy in 1940; that June German officials had proposed deporting Europe's Jews to the island, a scheme never carried out. To deny its ports to the Japanese navy and protect Allied shipping routes to India, Australia and South-East Asia, British forces seized the naval base of Diego-Suarez on 5 May 1942. A second campaign from 10 September took the capital, Tananarive, and fighting ended with an armistice on 6 November 1942. The island was then placed under Free French control.

units.bismarck_class_battleship: The Bismarck class comprised two fast battleships, Bismarck and Tirpitz, the largest and most powerful warships built for the German Kriegsmarine. Displacing more than 41,000 tonnes, each carried eight 38 cm (15 in) guns and could make 30 knots. In May 1941 Bismarck sank the battlecruiser HMS Hood in the Battle of the Denmark Strait and was then hunted down and sunk by the Royal Navy after a three-day chase. Tirpitz spent most of the war in Norwegian waters as a standing threat to the Arctic convoys until RAF Lancasters capsized her with Tallboy bombs in November 1944.
units.scharnhorst_class_battlecruiser: Scharnhorst and Gneisenau, commissioned by early 1939, were the first heavy warships of Nazi Germany's Kriegsmarine, variously classed as battleships or battlecruisers. Each carried nine 28 cm (11 in) guns in three triple turrets and could reach 31 knots. Together they raided Atlantic shipping, sank the carrier HMS Glorious off Norway on 8 June 1940, and dashed up the English Channel from France to Germany in early 1942. Gneisenau was put out of action by bombing at Kiel, and Scharnhorst was sunk at the Battle of North Cape in December 1943 by a force led by HMS Duke of York.
units.hipper_class_heavy_cruiser: The Admiral Hipper class comprised five heavy cruisers begun for the Kriegsmarine in the mid-1930s, of which only Admiral Hipper, Blücher and Prinz Eugen saw action; Lützow was sold unfinished to the Soviet Union and Seydlitz was never completed. They carried eight 20.3 cm (8 in) guns and twelve torpedo tubes and could make 32 knots. Blücher was sunk by Norwegian coastal defences outside Oslo in April 1940, while Admiral Hipper raided Atlantic shipping and fought at the Barents Sea in December 1942. Prinz Eugen sailed with Bismarck in 1941 and served until the war's end.
units.axis_destroyer_flotilla: Axis destroyer flotillas were groups of fast, torpedo-armed warships that screened battle fleets, escorted convoys and carried troops and supplies. Germany's large destroyers of the 1930s, armed from the Type 1936 onwards with 15 cm guns, suffered frequent trouble with their high-pressure machinery. Ten German destroyers landed mountain troops at Narvik in April 1940, and all were sunk or scuttled there, half the Kriegsmarine's destroyer strength. Most Italian destroyers of the 1930s were rated at over 38 knots, while Japanese destroyers carried the Type 93 'Long Lance' torpedo and ran the night supply runs the Allies called the Tokyo Express.
units.u_boat_flotilla: U-boat flotillas grouped the Kriegsmarine's submarines, which waged the war on Allied shipping in the Battle of the Atlantic. Their backbone was the medium Type VII, designed to attack the North Atlantic convoy lanes, of which 709 were commissioned. Karl Dönitz, commander of the U-boat arm, believed Britain could be defeated by attacking its convoys with coordinated groups of U-boats, the wolfpack tactic. The convoy offensive peaked in March 1943, but Allied countermeasures then made losses unsustainable, and after 'Black May' Dönitz called off the campaign on 24 May 1943.
units.axis_transport_convoy: Axis transport convoys carried troops and, late in the war, evacuees in merchant ships and requisitioned liners. They were vulnerable to submarines and aircraft, and losses could be very heavy. The largest effort was Operation Hannibal, from January to May 1945, in which between 494 and 1,080 vessels of every kind carried some 800,000 to 900,000 German civilians and 350,000 soldiers west across the Baltic ahead of the Red Army. Its worst loss came on 30 January 1945, when the Soviet submarine S-13 sank the transport Wilhelm Gustloff; by one estimate 9,343 people died.
units.axis_supply_convoy: Axis supply convoys carried vehicles, munitions and fuel from Italy to the Italian and German armies in Libya, escorted by Italian destroyers and torpedo boats. Malta, lying between Sicily and North Africa, was ideally placed to attack them. In November 1941 the Malta-based British Force K, guided by decrypted Axis signals, annihilated the Duisburg convoy without loss to itself, and British forces reading Italian naval codes went on intercepting later sailings. Escort work consumed about 75 per cent of the Italian navy's scarce fuel oil, and attacks from Malta disrupted Axis supplies just before the Second Battle of El Alamein.
units.littorio_class_battleship: The Littorio class, also called the Vittorio Veneto class, were Italy's most modern battleships: Littorio, Vittorio Veneto and Roma, with a fourth, Impero, never completed. Built between 1934 and 1942, they mounted nine 381 mm (15 in) guns and could make 30 knots. They formed the backbone of the Italian fleet in sorties against British convoys but were repeatedly torpedoed, Littorio at Taranto in November 1940 and Vittorio Veneto at Cape Matapan in March 1941. After the armistice of September 1943, German bombers sank Roma with Fritz X guided bombs as the fleet sailed for Malta.
units.zara_class_heavy_cruiser: The Zara class comprised four heavy cruisers, Zara, Fiume, Gorizia and Pola, built for the Italian Regia Marina between 1929 and 1932. They carried eight 203 mm (8 in) guns, could reach 32 knots and were among the best-protected heavy cruisers of the 1930s, though only by exceeding the Washington Naval Treaty's displacement limit. The class fought the Royal Navy at Calabria and Cape Matapan. At Matapan in March 1941 Pola was crippled by an aerial torpedo, and she, Zara and Fiume were sunk in a night action by three British battleships.
units.yamato_class_battleship: The Yamato class comprised Yamato and Musashi, commissioned in 1941 and 1942 and, at nearly 72,000 long tons fully loaded, the heaviest battleships ever built. Each carried nine 46 cm (18.1 in) guns, the largest naval artillery ever mounted on a warship, firing 1,460 kg shells over 42 km. A third hull became the aircraft carrier Shinano. Wary of American submarines and carriers, the Imperial Japanese Navy kept both battleships mostly in harbour; aircraft sank Musashi at Leyte Gulf in October 1944 and Yamato en route to Okinawa in April 1945.
units.shokaku_class_carrier: The Shokaku class comprised two aircraft carriers, Shokaku and Zuikaku, completed for the Imperial Japanese Navy shortly before the Pacific War and regarded as among the best carriers in the world. Capable of 34.5 knots, each operated around 72 aircraft. Apart from Midway, they fought in every major carrier action of the war, including Pearl Harbor, the Indian Ocean raid, the Coral Sea, the Eastern Solomons and Santa Cruz. An American submarine sank Shokaku during the Battle of the Philippine Sea in June 1944, and Zuikaku was sacrificed as a decoy off Cape Engaño in October 1944.
units.takao_class_heavy_cruiser: The Takao class comprised four heavy cruisers of the Imperial Japanese Navy, Takao, Atago, Maya and Chokai, launched in 1930 and 1931 and recognisable by their massive, almost battleship-like bridge. They carried ten 20.3 cm (8 in) guns in five twin turrets and a heavy torpedo armament, later firing the Type 93 oxygen torpedo. Chokai was Admiral Mikawa's flagship at the Battle of Savo Island in August 1942, where four Allied heavy cruisers were sunk. At Leyte Gulf in October 1944 American submarines sank Atago and Maya and crippled Takao, and Chokai was lost off Samar.
units.japanese_transport_convoy: Japanese transport convoys carried troops, fuel and supplies across widely scattered conquests and proved acutely vulnerable to Allied submarines and aircraft. American submarines alone accounted for 56 per cent of Japan's merchant shipping losses, and Allied submarines also sank many army troop transports. At the Battle of the Bismarck Sea in March 1943, American and Australian aircraft sank all eight transports and four destroyers of a convoy carrying 6,900 troops to Lae; only about 1,200 arrived. Japanese ships also carried Allied prisoners of war and Asian forced labourers in appalling conditions.
units.king_george_v_class_battleship: The King George V class were Britain's most modern battleships of the war: King George V, Prince of Wales, Duke of York, Anson and Howe, commissioned from 1940 to 1942. Each carried ten 14-inch guns and could make 28 knots. King George V and Prince of Wales took part in the action that ended with Bismarck's sinking in May 1941, and Duke of York was instrumental in sinking Scharnhorst in December 1943. Japanese bombers sank Prince of Wales on 10 December 1941, days after she reached Singapore, and in 1945 King George V and Howe bombarded Japanese targets.
units.illustrious_class_carrier: The Illustrious class comprised four Royal Navy aircraft carriers, Illustrious, Formidable, Victorious and Indomitable, laid down in the late 1930s as part of British rearmament. Unlike most carrier designs, they relied on an armoured flight deck and heavy anti-aircraft armament for protection, at the cost of a smaller air group. Victorious took part in the pursuit of Bismarck in 1941, while Illustrious and Formidable played prominent parts in the Mediterranean battles of 1940 and 1941. Indomitable was built to a modified design with an extra half-length hangar, and ships of the class served with the British Pacific Fleet in 1945.
units.town_class_cruiser: The Town class were ten light cruisers built for the Royal Navy in the 1930s within the limits of the London Naval Treaty, in three sub-groups: Southampton, Gloucester and Edinburgh. They carried twelve 6-inch guns in four triple turrets and could make about 32 knots, and were fitted with growing numbers of anti-aircraft guns and radar as the war went on. The class saw heavy service, including the action that sank the German battleship Scharnhorst in December 1943. Four ships, Edinburgh, Gloucester, Manchester and Southampton, were lost during the war.
units.allied_destroyer_flotilla: Destroyer flotillas were the workhorses of the Allied navies: fast, lightly armoured ships with guns, torpedoes and depth charges that screened fleets, escorted convoys, hunted submarines and fought surface actions. Standard British destroyers of 1939 displaced about 1,400 tons and carried four 4.7-inch guns and eight torpedo tubes. In April 1940 British destroyers, joined in the second action by the battleship Warspite, accounted for all ten German destroyers at Narvik, while six British and three French destroyers were lost at Dunkirk. In September 1940 the neutral United States transferred 50 older destroyers to Britain in exchange for bases.
units.flower_class_corvette_group: The Flower-class corvettes were small convoy escorts based on the design of the whale catcher Southern Pride, simple enough to be built quickly and cheaply in small merchant yards across Britain and Canada. In all 294 were completed, serving mainly with the Royal Navy and Royal Canadian Navy but also under other Allied flags. Armed with a 4-inch gun and depth charges, and later a Hedgehog anti-submarine mortar, they could make only 16 knots but were the mainstay of escort work in the Battle of the Atlantic. Thirty-three were lost, 22 of them to submarines.
units.liberty_ship_convoy: The Liberty ship was a simple, low-cost cargo ship of British origin that the United States adopted for mass production. Eighteen American shipyards built 2,710 of them between 1941 and 1945, an average of three every two days, using welded sections in place of riveting. The first, SS Patrick Henry, was launched by President Roosevelt; early ships took about 230 days to build, but by 1943 the median was 39 days. Capable of about 11 knots, they sailed in Allied convoys, and some were converted to carry troops for the North African landings.
units.troopship_convoy: Troopship convoys carried soldiers overseas, mostly in passenger liners requisitioned from commercial fleets, which loaded and unloaded in port rather than on beaches. Slower liners sailed in escorted convoys, while the fastest, such as Queen Mary and Queen Elizabeth, often sailed alone, relying on speed and zigzag courses to evade U-boats. Each Queen often carried as many as 15,000 men on a voyage, and by 1945 Queen Mary had carried over 800,000 troops. Losses could be terrible: the liner Lancastria, overloaded with troops evacuating France, was sunk on 17 June 1940 with the loss of several thousand lives.
units.iowa_class_battleship: The Iowa class were fast battleships ordered by the US Navy in 1939 and 1940, designed to the treaty limit of 45,000 long tons standard displacement. Four were completed, Iowa, New Jersey, Missouri and Wisconsin, each carrying nine 16-inch guns and capable of 33 knots; two further hulls remained unfinished at the war's end. Although designed for surface action, in the Pacific they served mainly as fast escorts for the Essex-class carriers of the Fast Carrier Task Force and bombarded Japanese positions. In September 1945 Japan's representatives signed the instrument of surrender aboard Missouri in Tokyo Bay.
units.essex_class_carrier: The Essex class were the US Navy's standard fleet carriers of the war, first authorised under the Two-Ocean Navy Act of 1940, with 32 eventually ordered. Each could make 33 knots and carry 90 to 100 aircraft, defended by twelve 5-inch guns and dozens of 40 mm and 20 mm anti-aircraft guns. From mid-1943 they formed the backbone of the US Navy and of its Fast Carrier Task Force in the Pacific. Fourteen saw combat before Japan's surrender, and although several were badly damaged by bombs, torpedoes and kamikaze attacks, none was sunk.
units.cleveland_class_cruiser: The Cleveland class were light cruisers built for the US Navy during the war, developed from the Brooklyn class with longer range, stronger anti-aircraft armament and better torpedo protection. Fifty-two were ordered, and nine hulls were completed instead as Independence-class light aircraft carriers. Each cruiser carried twelve 6-inch guns in four triple turrets and twelve 5-inch guns and could make 32.5 knots, with modern fire control and radar. The class served mainly in the Pacific, especially with the Fast Carrier Task Force, with some in the Atlantic, and every ship survived the war.
units.fletcher_class_destroyer_flotilla: The Fletcher class was designed in 1939, and 175 were commissioned by the US Navy during the war, more than any other destroyer class. The ships had a design speed of 38 knots and carried five 5-inch guns in single mounts and ten 21-inch torpedo tubes. Long-ranged and versatile, they served almost entirely in the Pacific in every destroyer role, from anti-submarine and anti-aircraft work to surface action, and accounted for 29 Japanese submarines. Nineteen were lost.
units.gato_class_submarine_flotilla: The Gato class was the first American submarine class of the war to be mass-produced, with 77 boats completed between 1940 and 1944. Designed as fleet submarines, they could make 21 knots surfaced and 9 knots submerged and were rated for a test depth of 300 feet. Together with the closely related Balao and Tench classes, they destroyed much of the Japanese merchant marine and a large part of the Imperial Japanese Navy. Twenty Gato-class boats were lost.
units.gangut_class_battleship: The Gangut class, also called the Sevastopol class, were the first dreadnought battleships of the Imperial Russian Navy, completed in 1914 and 1915 with twelve 12-inch guns in four triple turrets. Three were modernised by the Soviet Navy and renamed Marat, Oktyabrskaya Revolyutsiya and Parizhskaya Kommuna. In September 1941 Marat had her bow blown off and sank, but was raised and fought on as a floating battery through the Siege of Leningrad, while Oktyabrskaya Revolyutsiya was badly damaged by bombs. In the Black Sea, Parizhskaya Kommuna supported besieged Sevastopol and bombarded in support of the Kerch operations in early 1942.
units.kirov_class_cruiser: The Kirov class (Project 26) were six cruisers built for the Soviet Navy from 1935, the first large Soviet warships built from the keel up since the Civil War. Designed with help from Italy's Ansaldo and derived from the cruiser Raimondo Montecuccoli, they carried nine 180 mm guns and could make 36 knots. Two served in the Baltic and two in the Black Sea, bombarding Axis troops, and Kirov led the evacuation fleet from Tallinn to Leningrad in August 1941; the last pair was still being completed in the Far East. All six survived the war.
units.north_carolina_class_battleship: The North Carolina class comprised two fast battleships, North Carolina and Washington, built for the US Navy in the late 1930s and early 1940s. Designed under a treaty limit of 35,000 tons, they were rearmed during construction with nine 16-inch guns and could make 28 knots. Both served mainly in the Pacific, escorting fast carrier task forces, as at the Battle of the Philippine Sea, and bombarding shore positions. At the Naval Battle of Guadalcanal in November 1942 Washington's radar-directed guns fatally damaged the Japanese battleship Kirishima, and North Carolina survived a torpedo hit that year.
units.atomic_bomber_wing: Atomic bomber units flew specially modified Boeing B-29 Superfortresses, code-named Silverplate, adapted to carry the atomic bombs of the Manhattan Project. The only such unit, the US Army Air Forces' 509th Composite Group under Paul W. Tibbets, was activated in December 1944 and deployed to Tinian in May 1945. On 6 August 1945 its B-29 Enola Gay dropped the uranium bomb Little Boy on Hiroshima, and on 9 August Bockscar dropped the plutonium bomb Fat Man on Nagasaki. The two attacks killed an estimated 150,000 to 246,000 people by the end of the year, most of them civilians.
units.bf_109_squadron: The Messerschmitt Bf 109 was a single-seat fighter designed by Willy Messerschmitt and Robert Lusser, first flown in May 1935 and first used in combat in the Spanish Civil War. Its all-metal construction, enclosed cockpit, retractable undercarriage and liquid-cooled inverted-V12 engine made it one of the most advanced fighters of its day. Continually developed, it formed the backbone of the Luftwaffe's fighter force with the Fw 190 and fought on virtually every European front, flown by the highest-scoring German aces. Some 34,000 were built, more than any other fighter, part of them using concentration-camp slave labour.
units.fw_190_squadron: The Focke-Wulf Fw 190 was a single-seat fighter designed by Kurt Tank and powered in most versions by the BMW 801 radial engine, which let it carry heavier loads than the Bf 109. It began operations over France in August 1941 and proved superior in all but turning circle to the RAF's Spitfire Mk V until the improved Spitfire Mk IX arrived. Alongside the Bf 109 it became the backbone of the Luftwaffe's fighter arm, and it served widely as a fighter-bomber and ground-attack aircraft, largely replacing the Ju 87 by 1945. More than 20,000 were built.
units.ju_87_stuka_squadron: The Junkers Ju 87 Stuka was a German dive bomber, first flown in 1935 and first used in combat by the Condor Legion in Spain. Recognisable by its inverted gull wings, fixed spatted undercarriage and wind-driven sirens, it had automatic dive brakes to pull it out of its attack dive. It led the air assault on Poland in 1939 and was critical to the conquests of 1940, but its low speed and weak defensive armament meant it needed heavy fighter escort in the Battle of Britain. It later served as an anti-tank and anti-shipping aircraft; about 6,000 were built.
units.a6m_zero_squadron: The Mitsubishi A6M, the Navy Type 0 carrier fighter known to the Allies as Zeke or Zero, entered Imperial Japanese Navy service in 1940. It was then considered the most capable carrier fighter in the world, combining agility, speed, firepower and very long range, and it achieved an outstanding kill ratio early in the Pacific War. Its lack of armour and self-sealing fuel tanks left it vulnerable, and by mid-1942 new Allied tactics and aircraft met it on equal terms. Japan built 10,939, more than any other combat aircraft, and late in the war many were used in kamikaze attacks.
units.spitfire_squadron: The Supermarine Spitfire was a single-seat, short-range interceptor designed by R. J. Mitchell, distinguished by its thin elliptical wing and powered first by the Rolls-Royce Merlin and later by the Griffon. It entered RAF service in 1938 and was the only British fighter in continuous production throughout the war. In the Battle of Britain in 1940 the more numerous Hurricane flew more sorties, but Spitfire units suffered lower losses and achieved a higher victory-to-loss ratio. The Spitfire then became Fighter Command's principal fighter, serving as an interceptor, fighter-bomber and photo-reconnaissance aircraft in Europe, the Mediterranean and Asia.
units.p_51_mustang_squadron: The North American P-51 Mustang was a long-range single-seat fighter designed in 1940 at the request of the British Purchasing Commission, with the prototype completed in just 102 days. Early Allison-engined Mustangs lacked high-altitude performance, but fitting the Rolls-Royce Merlin transformed the design into the first long-range escort able to match the Luftwaffe's fighters. From late 1943 Mustangs escorted American bombers deep into Germany and helped secure Allied air superiority in 1944. The P-51D carried six .50-calibre machine guns under a bubble canopy, and Mustang pilots claimed 4,950 enemy aircraft destroyed.
units.sbd_dauntless_squadron: The Douglas SBD Dauntless was the US Navy's main carrier-based scout and dive bomber from 1940 to 1944, also flown by the Marine Corps. Long-ranged, good-handling and fitted with perforated dive brakes, it earned the nickname 'Slow But Deadly'. At the Coral Sea in May 1942 SBDs helped sink the light carrier Shoho, and at Midway in June 1942 they sank or fatally damaged all four Japanese fleet carriers present. Although the SB2C Helldiver was meant to replace it, the two fought side by side to the end; 5,936 were built.
units.lancaster_squadron: The Avro Lancaster was a four-engined heavy bomber designed by Roy Chadwick and powered by Rolls-Royce Merlins, entering RAF Bomber Command service in 1942. Its long, unobstructed bomb bay took the RAF's largest bombs, and it became the principal British heavy bomber of the night offensive against Germany, including the devastating raids on Hamburg in 1943. Lancasters of 617 Squadron breached the Möhne Dam with Barnes Wallis's bouncing bomb, and modified aircraft carried the 22,000 lb Grand Slam, the largest payload of the war. Lancasters flew some 156,000 sorties and dropped over 600,000 tons of bombs.
units.waffen_ss_division: The Waffen-SS was the armed combat branch of the Nazi Party's SS under Heinrich Himmler, growing from three regiments to over 38 divisions during the war. Founded on Nazi racial ideology, it later also enlisted volunteers and conscripts from occupied Europe, and combined front-line combat with police and security roles. Its units committed numerous atrocities, including murdering prisoners of war and civilians and taking part in the Holocaust. At Le Paradis in May 1940 Totenkopf Division troops machine-gunned 97 surrendered British soldiers, and at Oradour-sur-Glane in June 1944 a Das Reich Division company murdered 642 villagers, including women and children.
units.axis_naval_infantry_battalion: Axis naval infantry battalions were sailors and marines trained to fight ashore, seizing and defending ports, islands and coastlines. Italy's San Marco Regiment made landings on Adriatic islands during the invasion of Yugoslavia in April 1941, expanded to seven battalions, and fought at Tobruk, where its Tobruk Battalion helped repel a British commando landing in September 1942, and in Tunisia in 1943. Germany's navy landed a naval assault company from the old battleship Schleswig-Holstein to attack the Polish depot at Westerplatte on 1 September 1939, and by 1945 it had formed five naval infantry divisions from its own personnel.
units.wehrmacht_infantry_division: The infantry division was the mainstay of the German Army. An early-war division numbered some 17,000 men in three infantry regiments with an artillery regiment and supporting units, and unlike the panzer divisions it moved largely on foot and with horse-drawn transport; in 1941 some 60 to 70 per cent of the army's forces were not motorised. The infantry divisions followed the armoured spearheads to consolidate gains and mop up resistance. The army was also extensively involved in war crimes, including complicity in the Holocaust, the mass deaths of Soviet prisoners of war and reprisals against civilians.
units.panzer_division: The panzer division was the German Army's armoured division, a combined-arms formation with its own tanks, motorised infantry, artillery and support units that could act independently. The first three were formed on 15 October 1935, and there were 21 by the invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941. With tanks leading and the other arms in support, they were the key to the early blitzkrieg victories, though they had fewer and generally less advanced tanks than comparable Allied formations. As Allied doctrine caught up and shortages mounted their edge declined; the Waffen-SS and Luftwaffe also formed panzer divisions.
units.fallschirmjager_division: The Fallschirmjäger were the Luftwaffe's parachute troops, commanded by Kurt Student, and the first paratroops committed to large-scale airborne operations. Their first division, the 7th Air Division, was formed in 1938 and later became the 1st Parachute Division, and paratroops were dropped in Norway and the Netherlands in 1940. The invasion of Crete in May 1941, the first mainly airborne invasion in history, succeeded, but losses were so heavy that Hitler refused to authorise further large airborne operations. Thereafter the parachute divisions fought as elite ground troops, notably defending Monte Cassino from January to May 1944.
units.royal_marines_brigade: The Royal Marines, Britain's naval infantry, manned part of the guns in cruisers and battleships and crewed Britain's minor landing craft. Early in the war they formed an amphibiously trained Royal Marine Division, parts of which served at Dakar and in the capture of Madagascar, and in 1942 its battalions were reorganised as commandos. Nine Royal Marine Commandos, numbered 40 to 48, served in the Commando brigades in Sicily, Italy, Normandy, Walcheren and Burma. In January 1945 the Royal Marines also formed two conventional infantry brigades, the 116th and 117th.
