units.british_infantry_division: The infantry division was the basic fighting formation of the British Army, which raised 43 during the war, though not all existed at once. Its theoretical strength rose from 13,863 men in 1939 to 18,347 by 1944. A division had three infantry brigades with a reconnaissance regiment, a machine-gun battalion, engineers, medical and supply services, and an artillery group of three field regiments, each with twenty-four 25-pounders, plus anti-tank and light anti-aircraft regiments. British infantry divisions fought in France in 1940, in North Africa, including at El Alamein, in Burma and in North-West Europe.
units.chinese_infantry_division: The infantry division was the basic formation of China's National Revolutionary Army, which fought Japan from July 1937. A 1935 plan drawn up with German advisers aimed to raise 60 modern divisions of 9,000 to 10,000 men; some 30 had been reorganised by 1937, with the German-trained 87th and 88th Divisions as an elite core. Most divisions, though, lacked modern equipment, especially artillery, and were often severely under strength. From 1941 American Lend-Lease aid helped re-equip selected divisions, and Chinese divisions trained under General Joseph Stilwell fought beside the Allies in Burma.
units.soviet_guards_rifle_division: Guards rifle divisions were Soviet rifle divisions awarded the honorific title of Guards for distinguished service in battle. The title was introduced on 18 September 1941, when the 100th, 127th, 153rd and 161st Rifle Divisions became the 1st to 4th Guards Rifle Divisions for their part in the Yelnya offensive. Guards units received special colours and badges, double pay for ordinary soldiers and priority for equipment and replacements, though frequent use in offensives often left them under strength. By the war's end 117 rifle divisions had received the title, among more than 4,500 Guards units, formations and ships.
units.us_marine_division: The Marine division was the US Marine Corps' amphibious assault formation of the Pacific War. The Corps grew from two brigades to six divisions and five air wings, some 485,000 Marines, by the end of the war. The 1st Marine Division, activated aboard the battleship USS Texas in February 1941, landed on Guadalcanal on 7 August 1942, and Marine divisions went on to fight at Bougainville, Tarawa, Saipan, Guam, Tinian, Peleliu, Iwo Jima and Okinawa. Nearly 87,000 Marines became casualties during the war, including nearly 20,000 killed.
units.abwehr_agents: The Abwehr was the military intelligence service of the German armed forces, from 1938 attached to the Armed Forces High Command under Vice-Admiral Wilhelm Canaris, with stations across Germany, in neutral countries and in occupied territory. Its wartime record was poor: British intelligence ran some 19 double agents against it, among them the Spaniard Juan Pujol García, codenamed Garbo, and six saboteurs it sent to the United States in Operation Pastorius were executed. Hitler abolished the Abwehr in February 1944 and handed its work to the SS Reich Security Main Office; Canaris was executed shortly before the war's end.
units.sd_intelligence_cell: The Sicherheitsdienst (SD), the Security Service of the Reichsführer-SS, was the intelligence agency of the SS and the Nazi Party, founded in 1931 under Reinhard Heydrich to keep every individual in the Reich under continuous supervision. From 1939 it formed part of the Reich Security Main Office alongside the Gestapo. The SD staged the faked Polish attack on the Gleiwitz radio station used to justify invading Poland, and its Jewish affairs department drove the persecution of Germany's Jews. The Einsatzgruppen, which killed Jews, communists and others behind the German armies, were subordinated to it.
units.brandenburgers: The Brandenburgers were the Wehrmacht's special forces, raised in late 1939 as an arm of the Abwehr and expanded into a division in 1943. Many had lived abroad and spoke foreign languages, which let them infiltrate in disguise, as in the Netherlands in 1940, where they posed as Dutch barge crews. Ahead of the invasion of the Soviet Union they seized bridges and key installations, and they operated from Eastern Europe and the Caucasus to North Africa. Brandenburgers committed various atrocities, and late in the war parts of the unit fought partisans in Yugoslavia before it became a Panzergrenadier division.
units.kempeitai_operatives: The Kempeitai was the military police of the Imperial Japanese Army, founded in 1881 on the model of the French Gendarmerie, and it also acted as a secret and political police in Japan and the occupied territories, numbering about 35,000 by 1945. Besides enforcing military discipline, it handled counter-intelligence and counter-insurgency, issued travel permits and requisitioned labour and supplies. It ran prisoner-of-war and civilian internment camps where detainees were mistreated, procured so-called comfort women and human test subjects for Unit 731, and was notorious for torture, summary executions and massacres of civilians.
units.resistance_cell: Resistance cells were small clandestine groups of men and women who opposed the occupiers across German-occupied Europe, sometimes organised so that members of one cell did not know those of another. Their work ranged from non-cooperation, underground newspapers and hiding downed airmen to intelligence gathering, sabotage and guerrilla warfare; the Polish Home Army, the largest resistance movement, gave the Allies crucial intelligence on the V-2 rocket. Britain's SOE and the American OSS helped to create and supply many such groups. In June 1944 the French Resistance cut the railways at 486 points to hamper German movements after D-Day.
units.commandos: The Commandos were British special forces formed in June 1940 at Winston Churchill's request to raid German-occupied Europe, drawn first from army volunteers and later from all the services and from volunteers of occupied countries. Some 25,000 men passed through the Commando course at Achnacarry in Scotland. Their raids included the Lofoten Islands and, in March 1942, St Nazaire, where the explosive-laden destroyer Campbeltown wrecked the great Normandie dry dock at heavy cost to the raiders. Grown to over 30 units and four brigades, they later spearheaded Allied landings, including Normandy in June 1944.
units.photo_reconnaissance_flight: Photographic reconnaissance flights gathered intelligence by photographing enemy territory from the air. In the RAF the work was developed from 1939 by Sidney Cotton, who replaced slow Blenheims with Spitfires, later joined by de Havilland Mosquitos, adapted to fly higher and faster and painted in a special 'PRU Blue' camouflage. Their overlapping photographs were studied as stereoscopic images at RAF Medmenham, the main interpretation centre for Europe and the Mediterranean. This work made possible the August 1943 raid on the V-2 rocket plant at Peenemünde and the Crossbow attacks on V-1 sites in northern France.
units.soe_agents: The Special Operations Executive was a secret British organisation created in July 1940 to conduct espionage, sabotage and reconnaissance in occupied Europe and to aid resistance movements; Churchill told its minister, Hugh Dalton, to 'set Europe ablaze'. It directly employed or controlled more than 13,000 people, 3,200 of them women, and both men and women served as agents in occupied countries. SOE trained the Czechoslovak soldiers who assassinated Reinhard Heydrich in 1942, and in February 1943 Norwegian commandos of SOE destroyed the heavy-water plant at Vemork.
units.macchi_c202_squadron: The Macchi C.202 Folgore ('thunderbolt') was an Italian single-seat fighter designed by Mario Castoldi, developed from the C.200 Saetta and powered by an Italian-built Daimler-Benz DB 601 engine. It entered Regia Aeronautica service in July 1941 and soon proved an effective dogfighter, flying over Malta and North Africa and in smaller numbers on the Eastern Front. It is regarded as one of the best Italian fighters to serve in large numbers, and was flown by almost all of Italy's leading aces. About 1,150 were built, and after the armistice of 1943 the survivors were used mainly as trainers.
units.ki_43_oscar_squadron: The Nakajima Ki-43 Hayabusa ('Peregrine Falcon'), the Army Type 1 Fighter, was known to the Allies as 'Oscar', and American pilots often called it the 'Army Zero'. It entered Imperial Japanese Army Air Service squadrons in October 1941, just before the Pacific War, as the Army's first fighter with retractable undercarriage and an enclosed cockpit. Light and extremely manoeuvrable, it served on every front where the Army fought, but early versions lacked armour and self-sealing tanks and carried weak armament. Improved versions stayed in production until 1945, and 5,919 were built.
units.d3a_val_squadron: The Aichi D3A, the Navy Type 99 Carrier Bomber known to the Allies as 'Val', was the Imperial Japanese Navy's main dive bomber, recognisable by its elliptical wings and fixed undercarriage. It entered service in 1940 and took part in almost every Japanese naval action, including the attack on Pearl Harbor. In April 1942 D3As sank the British carrier Hermes in the Indian Ocean, and later that year they helped sink the US carriers Lexington, Yorktown and Hornet; the type sank more Allied warships than any other Axis aircraft. About 1,500 were built.
units.italian_infantry_division: After a 1938 reorganisation, Italian infantry divisions were 'binary' divisions, built around two infantry regiments instead of three, with an artillery regiment, a mortar battalion, an engineer battalion and support units. When Italy entered the war on 10 June 1940 its army had 59 infantry divisions, alongside Blackshirt, Alpine, mobile, motorised and armoured divisions. Much of their artillery was obsolete and far too dependent on horse transport. The army fought in France, Greece, North Africa and the Soviet Union, and after the armistice of September 1943 it split between the Allied and Axis sides.
units.alpini_division: The Alpini were Italy's mountain infantry, founded in 1872. Italy fielded six Alpine divisions in the war, each of two Alpini regiments and an Alpine artillery regiment, some 17,460 men with almost 5,000 mules. In 1942 the Tridentina, Julia and Cuneense divisions went to the Soviet Union, where, equipped for mountain warfare, they were made to hold a front on the open plains of the Don. Encircled in January 1943, the Tridentina broke out at Nikolayevka on 26 January, but only about a third of it and a tenth of the Julia survived, and the Cuneense was annihilated.
units.japanese_infantry_division: The infantry division was the principal formation of the Imperial Japanese Army. The first 18 divisions were raised as 'square' divisions, but most formed after 1938 were triangular, with three infantry regiments. A standard division numbered about 19,770 men, with a field or mountain artillery regiment, a cavalry or reconnaissance regiment, engineers, medical units and a transport regiment using carts, pack horses or trucks. At the time of Pearl Harbor 50 divisions were serving abroad, most in China. Throughout the war the army committed numerous atrocities against civilians and prisoners of war, the Nanjing Massacre being the best known.
units.snlf_brigade: The Special Naval Landing Forces were the naval infantry of the Imperial Japanese Navy, known in the West as Japanese marines. The Shanghai SNLF, formed in October 1932, was the first official unit, and SNLF units fought throughout the war in China. Most were single battalions of 200 to over 3,000 men, and some were trained as paratroops. After failing to take Milne Bay in New Guinea they became mainly a defensive force, and at Tarawa in 1943 about 1,700 men of the 7th Sasebo SNLF, with 2,000 base personnel, inflicted over 3,000 US Marine casualties.
units.hurricane_squadron: The Hawker Hurricane was a single-seat monoplane fighter designed by Sydney Camm, first flown in November 1935 and in RAF squadron service from December 1937. Powered by the Rolls-Royce Merlin and built by conventional methods that eased production and repair, it equipped 18 RAF squadrons when war broke out. Although the Spitfire drew more public attention, Hurricanes inflicted about 60 per cent of the Luftwaffe's losses in the Battle of Britain. It went on to serve as a fighter-bomber and ground-attack aircraft and at sea as the Sea Hurricane; 14,487 were built in Britain and Canada.
units.f4f_wildcat_squadron: The Grumman F4F Wildcat was an American carrier fighter that entered service in 1940 with the US Navy and, as the Martlet, with the Royal Navy, which first took it into combat. At the time of Pearl Harbor it was the best fighter the US Navy and Marine Corps had, and it fought the Zero at the Coral Sea and Midway. Outperformed by the Zero, its pilots relied on close mutual-support tactics and claimed a kill-to-loss ratio of 5.9 to 1 in 1942. The Wildcat also pioneered fighter operations from escort carriers.
units.f6f_hellcat_squadron: The Grumman F6F Hellcat was an American carrier fighter designed to replace the Wildcat and beat the Zero, powered by the 2,000 hp Pratt & Whitney R-2800 Double Wasp. It first saw combat over Marcus Island on 31 August 1943 and became the US Navy's dominant fighter in the second half of the Pacific War, including at the Battle of the Philippine Sea, which aircrews called the 'Great Marianas Turkey Shoot'. Hellcats were credited with 5,223 enemy aircraft, more than any other Allied naval aircraft, and 12,275 were built in just over two years.
units.tbf_avenger_squadron: The Grumman TBF Avenger was an American carrier-based torpedo bomber, also built by General Motors' Eastern Aircraft Division as the TBM, which produced most of them. It entered service in 1942 and had a costly debut at Midway, where five of the six Avengers engaged were lost. It became the most widely used torpedo bomber of the war, helping to sink numerous warships including the battleships Yamato and Musashi. Avengers were also among the most effective submarine hunters in both the Atlantic and the Pacific, with about 30 kills.
units.yak_9_squadron: The Yakovlev Yak-9 was a single-seat Soviet fighter developed from the Yak-7B, reaching fighter regiments in late 1942. Its lighter metal structure allowed more fuel and armament than earlier Yaks built from wood, and it was manoeuvrable and easy to control at low and medium altitudes. It helped the Soviet air forces regain air superiority at Kursk in 1943, and variants included the Yak-9T with a 37 mm cannon and the long-range Yak-9D. It also equipped the Free French Normandie-Niémen unit; 14,579 were built during the war.
units.il_2_sturmovik_squadron: The Ilyushin Il-2 Shturmovik was a Soviet ground-attack aircraft whose armour formed a load-bearing part of its airframe. Known to the soldiers it supported as the 'Flying Tank', it entered service in 1941 and played a crucial role on the Eastern Front. Stalin told factory managers the Il-2 was 'as essential to the Red Army as air and bread'. With 36,183 built during the war, it was one of the most produced military aircraft of all time.
units.p_40_warhawk_squadron: The Curtiss P-40 was an American single-seat fighter-bomber developed from the P-36 Hawk, first flown in 1938 and known in British and Commonwealth service as the Tomahawk and Kittyhawk. Its Allison engine lacked a two-speed supercharger, leaving it outclassed at high altitude, so it was rarely used over northwest Europe. Between 1941 and 1944 it played a critical role in North Africa, the Southwest Pacific and China, where the American Volunteer Group, the Flying Tigers, flew it against the Japanese. By November 1944, when production ended, 13,738 had been built.
units.dewoitine_d520_squadron: The Dewoitine D.520 was a French single-seat fighter that entered service in early 1940, designed to a 1936 requirement for a fast, modern fighter built around a 20 mm cannon and the Hispano-Suiza 12Y engine. Slower than the Bf 109E but more manoeuvrable, it came close to matching the latest German types, but production delays meant too few reached squadrons to affect the Battle of France. After the armistice it served with both Vichy and Free French forces and returned to production in 1942. About 900 were built.
units.allied_naval_infantry_battalion: Allied naval infantry battalions were sailors and marines organised to fight ashore, in amphibious landings and in the defence of ports and naval bases. The Soviet Navy sent some 350,000 sailors to fight on land, formed into about 40 naval infantry brigades and six regiments of 650-man battalions, many drawn from surplus ships' crews. They fought at Odessa, Moscow, Leningrad, Sevastopol, Stalingrad, Novorossiysk and Kerch, made more than 114 landings, and in 1945 landed in Korea, southern Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands. Britain's Royal Marines and the US Marine Corps provided naval infantry of their own.
units.us_infantry_division: The infantry division was the basic combat formation of the US Army. Between late 1939 and early 1942 the Army reorganised its divisions from the old 'square' pattern into 'triangular' divisions controlling three infantry regiments, with divisional artillery and supporting units. Some 89 divisions were active by 1945, most of them infantry, and it became standard practice to attach a separate tank battalion to each infantry division where possible. Six infantry divisions were converted to motorised divisions in 1942, but all reverted, since a standard division had enough transport if trucks were taken from other duties.
units.us_armored_division: The US Army's armored divisions combined tanks, infantry and artillery in flexible combined-arms groupings called Combat Command A, Combat Command B and Combat Command Reserve. Plans in 1942 foresaw as many as 46 armored divisions, but shipping shortages and doubts about the balance of forces limited the total to 16. In 1943 most were reorganised on lighter lines, with three tank battalions instead of six and 263 tanks instead of 390, though the 2nd and 3rd Armored Divisions kept the older, heavier structure. Their main tank, the M4 Sherman, was outperformed by German tanks that began appearing in 1943.
units.soviet_rifle_division: The rifle division was the basic infantry formation of the Red Army, organised since 1922 around three rifle regiments. Its 1941 wartime establishment was 14,483 men with 10,420 rifles, but only 20 divisions on the western border had reached that strength when Germany invaded. Some 480 rifle divisions were raised during the Great Patriotic War, many destroyed and re-formed more than once under the same number, and at least 42 'national' divisions were formed, among them Azeri, Armenian and Georgian rifle divisions. Divisions that distinguished themselves could be raised to Guards status.
units.guards_tank_corps: The Soviet tank corps, re-formed from March 1942 to mass tanks for decisive operations, was despite its title roughly the size of a German panzer division. It grew to three tank brigades and a motor rifle brigade, later with self-propelled gun regiments, and tank corps were the building blocks of the Soviet tank armies. Of 31 tank corps formed during the war, 12 earned the Guards title. The 24th Tank Corps, for example, became the 2nd Guards Tatsinskaya Tank Corps during its raid on Tatsinskaya in December 1942, which destroyed many Luftwaffe transport aircraft.
units.french_infantry_division: The infantry division was the backbone of the French Army in May 1940, when France fielded 117 divisions, 104 of them for the defence of the north. After the German breakthrough at Sedan, three French field armies were trapped in the north with the British and Belgians, and France signed an armistice on 22 June 1940. In Italy the French Expeditionary Corps under General Alphonse Juin, four divisions largely of Moroccan and Algerian troops led by French officers, broke through the Gustav Line in May 1944, though its record was marred by numerous crimes against Italian civilians.
units.commonwealth_division: Commonwealth divisions were raised by Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, South Africa and other parts of the British Empire to fight alongside British forces. At the Second Battle of El Alamein in late 1942, Australian, New Zealand, South African and Indian divisions fought beside British formations. Australia's 9th Division fought at Tobruk and El Alamein before serving in New Guinea and Borneo, and the 1st Canadian Division fought in Sicily and Italy, notably at Ortona. The Indian Army grew from under 200,000 men in 1939 to over 2.5 million by August 1945, the largest volunteer army in history.

facilities.headquarters: The seat of a side's supreme command: the staffs, signals and planning offices that direct its armies, fleets and air forces across every theatre. A General Headquarters is the most defended installation a side possesses, and the territory that holds it is the one its enemies most want to take. Holding the enemy's headquarters territory is among the conditions of victory.
facilities.shipyard: A naval yard of slipways, dry docks and fitting-out basins where warships, submarines, transports and aircraft are built. Every ship and air squadron a side puts to sea or into the air comes from one. Two yards in the same territory build twice as fast as one, three three times as fast, and so on.
facilities.training_facility: A training depot where recruits are drilled, equipped and formed into divisions, brigades and battalions, and where special forces and agents are prepared for their work. Two depots in the same territory train twice as fast as one, three three times as fast, and so on.
facilities.construction_yard: An engineer corps of surveyors, builders and heavy plant, able to raise mines, refineries, depots, yards and defences wherever its side holds ground. No territory can be built up or fortified without one within reach. Two in the same territory build twice as fast as one, three three times as fast, and so on.
facilities.advanced_shipyard: A fleet base: a naval yard enlarged and modernised with the lessons of the war, able to build ships and air squadrons more efficiently than a standard yard. It becomes available only through naval design research. Wartime American yards built Liberty ships in weeks by prefabricating whole sections and welding them together rather than riveting.
facilities.advanced_training_facility: An army training centre where the latest doctrine, weapons and tactics are taught, forming troops and special forces more efficiently than a standard depot. It becomes available only through army doctrine research. Such schools trained soldiers under live fire, with exercises modelled on the fighting of the moment, so that recruits met the noise and confusion of battle before they met the enemy.
facilities.advanced_construction_yard: A construction battalion of experienced military engineers with modern equipment, raising installations and defences more efficiently than a standard engineer corps. It becomes available only through fortification design research. The United States Navy's construction battalions, the Seabees, formed in 1942, were such a force, building airfields, harbours and bases across the Pacific, often under fire.
facilities.mine: A working mine: coal, iron ore, bauxite, oil or whatever else the territory's ground holds, dug and brought to the surface. Raw materials are worth nothing until a refinery turns them into war materiel, but a refinery on any territory a side controls will draw on a mine on any other.
facilities.refinery: A refinery, mill or foundry that turns raw materials into war materiel: steel, fuel, rubber and the other stuff of which every ship, aircraft, division and installation is made. It need not stand beside a mine; a refinery on any territory a side controls works the output of mines on any other.
facilities.minefield: Sea mines laid across the approaches to a territory's coast and harbours. Warships that come in close to bombard the shore risk being struck and crippled, their guns put out of action before they can do their work. Both sides laid mines in great numbers; in 1945 American B-29 bombers flying at night mined the approaches to Japan's home ports.
facilities.coastal_battery: Heavy guns emplaced on the shore to defend a coast and its harbours. A battery fires on enemy warships that stand in to bombard the territory, and on troops that try to come ashore in an assault. Germany's Atlantic Wall, along the coasts of occupied Europe and Norway, organised its heavy guns into more than 800 batteries.
facilities.fortifications: Field works and permanent defences: bunkers, pillboxes, trenches, wire and obstacles covering the beaches and approaches. Fortifications shelter a territory from bombardment, and a territory with two or more of them cannot be assaulted until enough have been destroyed, by bombardment or by sabotage.
facilities.hardened_airbase: An airfield with bomb-proof shelters, dispersal areas and hardened stores, built to protect aircraft on the ground from air attack. It shelters the strategic bomber force while it is based there. Aircraft caught on the ground can be lost as surely as in the air, and in the Battle of Britain the Luftwaffe turned its attacks on the RAF's airfields.
facilities.heavy_coastal_battery: A coastal battery of the largest calibre, its guns in concrete casemates or armoured turrets and able to engage warships at long range. Like a standard battery it fires on ships that bombard the territory and on troops that try to land, and it becomes available only through fortification design research.
facilities.fortress_line: A continuous fortified line of the kind built along frontiers before and during the war: underground galleries, turrets, casemates and anti-tank obstacles in depth. It shelters a territory from bombardment more strongly than ordinary fortifications, counts as a fortification against assault, and becomes available only through fortification design research.

missions.diplomacy: Envoys are sent to a neutral or friendly territory to win its people and leaders over with promises, pressure and aid. Success shifts the territory's population toward the sending side, and a neutral territory may come over to that side entirely. The territory must not be in revolt. The envoy's diplomacy rating decides the outcome.
missions.rescue: A daring raid to free a comrade held prisoner by the enemy, whether in an enemy territory or aboard an enemy fleet. The team must reach the prisoner where they are held; the combat skill of those taking part decides whether they bring the prisoner out.
missions.sabotage: Saboteurs slip into enemy territory to destroy one target: an installation, a ship, an air squadron, a division or a special forces unit, so long as it is complete and not at sea. Sabotage can reach defences that bombardment cannot. Both combat skill and espionage count.
missions.espionage: Agents gather intelligence on a territory: what its factories, yards and defences hold. Against an enemy or neutral territory it gives an accurate picture that grows stale as time passes. Run on a territory of one's own, it becomes counter-intelligence, helping to catch enemy agents at work there. The agent's espionage rating decides the outcome.
missions.reconnaissance: An aerial or ground reconnaissance of a territory not under one's control, even one never explored: its installations, forces, resources, the mood of its population and who controls it. It does not reveal the people or special forces present, nor what its factories are building. Only reconnaissance units may carry it out.
missions.recruitment: A leading figure travels to a friendly territory to win a new officer, official or agent to the side's cause. Only a major figure may undertake it, and success depends in part on how firmly the territory stands with the side. It may be repeated.
missions.abduction: A team is sent to seize a named enemy figure alive, wherever they are: in a territory or aboard a fleet, so long as they are not at sea and not already a prisoner. Capturing the enemy's leaders is among the conditions of victory. Combat skill decides the outcome.
missions.ship_design_research: A figure with the knowledge for it works with the designers at a friendly naval yard to hasten new ship and aircraft designs. Research goes on slowly at every yard even without such help, but a research mission brings results much sooner. A new design is available the moment it is ready.
missions.facility_design_research: A figure with the knowledge for it works with the engineers of a friendly engineer corps to hasten new designs for installations and defences. Research goes on slowly wherever engineers work, but a research mission brings results much sooner, and a new design is available the moment it is ready.
missions.troop_training_research: A figure with the knowledge for it works with the instructors of a friendly training depot to develop new doctrine and new kinds of formation. Research goes on slowly at every depot, but a research mission brings results much sooner, and new formations are available the moment they are ready.
missions.incite_uprising: Agents and local sympathisers are organised against the enemy's hold on one of its territories: strikes, sabotage, hidden arms and open revolt. Resistance weakens the enemy's hold, puts its troops, installations and officers there at risk, and makes it easier for captured comrades to escape. Leadership decides the outcome.
missions.sabotage_atomic_program: An attack on the enemy's atomic bomber force where its location is known and it is not in the air or at sea. Success destroys it before it can be used. Only the Axis may attempt it, and both combat skill and espionage count.
missions.subdue_uprising: A leading figure is sent to restore order in a friendly territory in revolt, by negotiation, reforms or force. Success ends or eases the unrest and restores the territory to its side. Leadership decides the outcome. In the occupied and contested lands of the war, restoring order meant garrisons and curfews, but also food, work and the courting of local leaders.
missions.assassination: An attempt on the life of a named enemy figure. The leaders on whom victory turns cannot be killed, but they can be wounded, which makes them easier to capture. Combat skill decides the outcome. Among the war's attempts was Operation Anthropoid, in which Czechoslovak soldiers trained in Britain fatally wounded Reinhard Heydrich in Prague in 1942.

characters.hitler: Adolf Hitler, born in Braunau am Inn, Austria-Hungary, in 1889, served in the German Army in the First World War and later led the Nazi Party. Appointed Chancellor of Germany in January 1933, he made himself dictator after President Hindenburg's death in 1934. His expansionist policy was the primary cause of the war in Europe, which began with his invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939; in June 1941 he invaded the Soviet Union. His regime carried out the Holocaust, the genocide of about six million Jews, and killed millions of other civilians and prisoners of war. He killed himself in Berlin on 30 April 1945.
characters.mussolini: Benito Mussolini founded the Fascist movement in 1919 and became Prime Minister of Italy after the March on Rome in 1922, making the country a one-party dictatorship. He waged a war of conquest in Ethiopia from 1935 in which his forces used poison gas, allied with Hitler in 1936, and took Italy into the Second World War in June 1940. After defeats in Africa and the Allied landing in Sicily, the King dismissed and arrested him in July 1943. Freed by German troops at Gran Sasso, he headed the Italian Social Republic, a German puppet state in the north, until partisans captured and executed him on 28 April 1945.
characters.tojo: Hideki Tojo, a career officer of the Imperial Japanese Army, was chief of staff of the Kwantung Army in 1937 when Japan invaded China. As Minister of the Army from 1940 he backed the pact with Germany and Italy, and in October 1941 Emperor Hirohito appointed him Prime Minister. His cabinet took Japan to war with the attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, and used the military police to suppress dissent at home. His government presided over widespread war crimes, including the massacre and starvation of prisoners of war and civilians. He was forced to resign in July 1944 after the fall of Saipan.
characters.goring: Hermann Göring was a First World War fighter ace and an early Nazi, wounded in Hitler's failed Munich putsch of 1923. After 1933 he oversaw the creation of the Gestapo, commanded the Luftwaffe and, as head of the Four Year Plan from 1936, mobilised the economy for war. Hitler named him his successor in 1939, and in July 1941 Göring ordered Reinhard Heydrich to organise the practical details of the Final Solution, the murder of Europe's Jews. His standing fell as the Luftwaffe failed to stop Allied bombing or supply Stalingrad, and in April 1945 Hitler stripped him of all posts and ordered his arrest.
characters.goebbels: Joseph Goebbels, who held a doctorate in philology from Heidelberg, became the Nazi Party's leader in Berlin in 1926. As Reich Minister of Propaganda from 1933 he controlled the press, radio, film and the arts, and used them to spread the regime's antisemitism. He incited the Kristallnacht pogrom of November 1938, pressed for the deportation of Berlin's Jews and knew of their extermination. From 1943 he campaigned for total war, and in July 1944 Hitler gave him charge of mobilising civilians for it. After Hitler's death he served one day as Chancellor, and on 1 May 1945 he and his wife poisoned their six children and killed themselves.
characters.himmler: Heinrich Himmler joined the Nazi Party in 1923 and in 1929 became head of the SS, which he built from a small bodyguard unit into one of the most powerful institutions in Germany. He came to control the police, including the Gestapo, and the Waffen-SS, and from 1943 was also Minister of the Interior. As the principal enforcer of the regime's racial policies he ran the concentration and extermination camps and formed the Einsatzgruppen death squads, making him a chief architect of the Holocaust. In 1945 he sought peace talks with the Western Allies behind Hitler's back, was dismissed, and killed himself in British custody on 23 May 1945.
characters.canaris: Wilhelm Canaris, a naval officer who carried out clandestine work in Spain during the First World War, became head of the Abwehr, Germany's military intelligence service, on 1 January 1935. Initially a supporter of Hitler, he turned against the regime after the invasion of Poland and engaged in both passive and active resistance, working alongside his deputy Hans Oster. In December 1940 he carried Hitler's demands to Franco and reported that Spain would not enter the war until Britain was defeated. Dismissed in February 1944 and arrested after the July plot, he was hanged at Flossenbürg concentration camp on 9 April 1945.
characters.speer: Albert Speer, an architect, joined the Nazi Party in 1931 and entered Hitler's inner circle, designing the Reich Chancellery and the party rally grounds at Nuremberg. As General Building Inspector for Berlin from 1937 he was responsible for the office that evicted Jewish tenants from their homes. In February 1942 he succeeded Fritz Todt as armaments minister and head of the Organisation Todt, and promoted himself as the author of an armaments miracle. His factories and building projects relied heavily on forced and slave labour, including through the fighter production staff he set up in 1944.
characters.rommel: Erwin Rommel won the Pour le Mérite on the Italian front in the First World War and published his tactical study Infantry Attacks in 1937. He commanded the 7th Panzer Division in the invasion of France in 1940, and from February 1941 led German and Italian forces in North Africa, where he became known as the Desert Fox. Made a field marshal after taking Tobruk in June 1942, he was defeated by Montgomery at El Alamein that November. In 1944 he commanded Army Group B against the Normandy invasion. Implicated in the July plot against Hitler, he was forced to take poison on 14 October 1944.
characters.guderian: Heinz Guderian, a leading developer of German armoured warfare, set out his ideas in Achtung - Panzer! in 1937. After leading an armoured corps in Poland, he broke the French line at Sedan in May 1940. He commanded the 2nd Panzer Army in the invasion of the Soviet Union, where his troops carried out the Commissar Order to shoot captured Soviet political officers, and was relieved in December 1941 after a dispute with Hitler. Recalled in 1943 as Inspector General of Armoured Troops, he became acting Chief of the Army General Staff after the July 1944 plot and sat on the court of honour that expelled suspected plotters.
characters.manstein: Erich von Manstein devised the plan for the 1940 attack on France through the Ardennes, which Hitler adopted over the army's original scheme. In the invasion of the Soviet Union he commanded the 11th Army in the Crimea, where his command supplied Einsatzgruppe D with vehicles and fuel while it murdered Jews, and he was promoted to field marshal on 1 July 1942 after the siege of Sevastopol. His attempt to relieve the Sixth Army at Stalingrad failed in December 1942, but his counteroffensive at Kharkov in early 1943 regained much ground. Disputes with Hitler led to his dismissal in March 1944.
characters.kesselring: Albert Kesselring, a Bavarian artillery officer, moved to the aviation ministry in 1933 and helped build the Luftwaffe, serving as its chief of staff from 1936 to 1938. He commanded air fleets in Poland, France, the Battle of Britain and the invasion of the Soviet Union before becoming Commander-in-Chief South in the Mediterranean in November 1941. In Italy he fought a long defensive campaign on lines such as the Gustav Line, and in June 1944 he authorised measures of the utmost severity against partisans and reprisals against civilians, after which his troops carried out a series of massacres. In March 1945 he replaced Rundstedt as Commander-in-Chief West.
characters.donitz: Karl Dönitz commanded a U-boat in the First World War and was captured in 1918, experience that led him to the idea of submarines attacking in groups, the wolfpack. He led the U-boat arm in the Battle of the Atlantic, and in January 1943 succeeded Raeder as commander-in-chief of the navy with the rank of grand admiral. The U-boats lost the initiative from May 1943, yet he kept them fighting; about 30,000 of the 40,000 men who served in them died. A dedicated Nazi, he was named Hitler's successor as head of state on 30 April 1945 and authorised Germany's unconditional surrender on 7 May.
characters.raeder: Erich Raeder served as chief of staff to Admiral Hipper in the First World War and took part in the Battles of Dogger Bank and Jutland. He became head of the navy in 1928, remained its commander-in-chief when it was renamed the Kriegsmarine in 1935, and was made grand admiral in 1939. Believing the fleet unready for war, he used surface ships as commerce raiders, and in October 1939 brought Hitler the proposal to invade Norway, a campaign that cost the navy heavily in cruisers and destroyers. After Hitler's outrage over the Battle of the Barents Sea, he was replaced by Karl Dönitz in January 1943.
characters.skorzeny: Otto Skorzeny, a Vienna-born civil engineer and early member of the Austrian Nazi movement, joined the Waffen-SS after the Luftwaffe turned him down. After fighting on the Eastern Front, he was given command of an SS special operations unit in April 1943. He tracked down the imprisoned Mussolini and was present at the Gran Sasso raid that freed him in September 1943, and in October 1944 he kidnapped the son of the Hungarian regent Miklós Horthy to force the regent from power. In the Ardennes offensive of December 1944 he led Operation Greif, in which German soldiers in American uniforms infiltrated Allied lines.
characters.yamamoto: Isoroku Yamamoto lost two fingers at the Battle of Tsushima in 1905, and later studied at Harvard and served as naval attaché in Washington, experience that convinced him Japan could not match American industrial power. An early champion of naval aviation, he opposed the pact with Germany and Italy while vice minister of the navy. As commander-in-chief of the Combined Fleet from 1939 he planned the surprise attack on Pearl Harbor of December 1941. After the defeat at Midway in June 1942 and the loss of Guadalcanal, he was killed on 18 April 1943 when American fighters, guided by decoded messages, shot down his aircraft over Bougainville.
characters.nagumo: Chuichi Nagumo was an admiral of the Imperial Japanese Navy who commanded the main carrier striking force, the Kido Butai, in the attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941. In the following months his carriers bombed Darwin in Australia and raided the British Eastern Fleet in the Indian Ocean. At Midway in June 1942 his force lost four fleet carriers in a crushing defeat. He then commanded the carriers of the Third Fleet at the Battles of the Eastern Solomons and Santa Cruz Islands before taking a naval command in the Mariana Islands, where he killed himself during the Battle of Saipan in July 1944.
characters.yamashita: Tomoyuki Yamashita commanded the Twenty-Fifth Army in the invasion of Malaya, taking the peninsula and Singapore in 70 days; at Singapore's fall on 15 February 1942 some 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops were captured. The occupation that followed included the Sook Ching massacre of Chinese civilians. Sidelined to Manchukuo in July 1942, he was recalled in October 1944 to defend the Philippines with the Fourteenth Area Army. Japanese forces there under his overall command committed widespread atrocities against civilians and prisoners, and his troops held out in northern Luzon until Japan's formal surrender on 2 September 1945.
characters.graziani: Rodolfo Graziani, a committed Fascist, led Italian colonial campaigns in Libya and Ethiopia in the 1920s and 1930s, where his methods included concentration camps that caused many civilian deaths and, in Ethiopia, the use of poison gas. As Viceroy of Ethiopia he ordered brutal reprisals after an attempt on his life in February 1937, known as Yekatit 12. In September 1940 his 10th Army invaded Egypt, but the British counteroffensive that December routed his forces and he resigned. After Italy's armistice in 1943 he was the only Marshal of Italy to stay loyal to Mussolini, serving as defence minister of the Italian Social Republic.
characters.ciano: Galeazzo Ciano, son of the Fascist admiral Costanzo Ciano, married Mussolini's daughter Edda in 1930 and became Foreign Minister in 1936 after serving in the Ethiopian war. Widely seen as Mussolini's likely successor, he signed the Pact of Steel with Germany in May 1939, though he grew disenchanted with Germany. As defeats mounted he urged Italy's exit from the war, and in 1943 he was moved to the post of ambassador to the Holy See. He voted against Mussolini in the Grand Council in July 1943, was later handed to the Italian Social Republic, and was shot after the Verona trial on 11 January 1944.
characters.churchill: Winston Churchill served as a soldier and war correspondent before entering Parliament in 1900, and was First Lord of the Admiralty in the First World War and later Chancellor of the Exchequer. Out of office in the 1930s, he warned against Nazi Germany and called for rearmament. He returned to the Admiralty when war broke out and became Prime Minister in May 1940, leading a national coalition that kept Britain fighting after the fall of France. He agreed the Atlantic Charter with Roosevelt in August 1941 and met Roosevelt and Stalin at Tehran and Yalta. His party lost the general election of 1945.
characters.roosevelt: Franklin D. Roosevelt, left paralysed in the legs by illness in 1921, was elected President of the United States in 1932 and met the Great Depression with the New Deal. Re-elected in 1936 and 1940, he sent aid to Britain and China through Lend-Lease. After Pearl Harbor he led the country into war, mobilised its economy, adopted a Europe-first strategy and started the programme to build the atomic bomb; in February 1942 he also signed the order under which Japanese Americans were interned. Elected to a fourth term in 1944, he met Churchill and Stalin at Yalta and died in office on 12 April 1945.
characters.stalin: Joseph Stalin, a Georgian-born Bolshevik, became General Secretary of the Communist Party in 1922 and by the 1930s was dictator of the Soviet Union. Forced collectivisation contributed to the famine of 1932-33, and in the Great Purge over a million people were imprisoned and at least 700,000 executed. In 1939 he made a pact with Nazi Germany and joined in the invasion of Poland, and in 1940 his secret police shot some 22,000 Polish prisoners at Katyn. After Germany attacked in June 1941 he led the war effort as Supreme Commander, met Churchill and Roosevelt at Tehran and Yalta, and saw the Red Army take Berlin in 1945.
characters.chiang_kai_shek: Chiang Kai-shek, commandant of the Whampoa Military Academy from 1924, took control of the Nationalist party and army after Sun Yat-sen's death and largely unified China in the Northern Expedition of 1926 to 1928. In April 1927 he turned on his Communist allies in the Shanghai massacre. Detained by his own generals in the Xi'an Incident of 1936, he then formed a united front with the Communists and from 1937 led China's resistance to Japan from Chongqing. In 1938 his retreating army destroyed Yellow River dykes to slow the Japanese, a flood that killed an estimated 800,000 to one million people. He met Roosevelt and Churchill at Cairo in 1943.
characters.de_gaulle: Charles de Gaulle was wounded and captured at Verdun in 1916, and between the wars he argued for mobile armoured forces. In May 1940 he led the 4th Armoured Division in counterattacks at Montcornet and Abbeville, and was then made Under-Secretary of State for War. Rejecting the armistice, he went to London and on 18 June 1940 appealed to the French to continue the fight, for which a Vichy court martial condemned him to death in absentia. He led the Free French Forces and then the French Committee of National Liberation, and from June 1944 headed the Provisional Government of the French Republic.
characters.eisenhower: Dwight D. Eisenhower graduated from West Point in 1915 and served between the wars in staff posts, including as an aide to Douglas MacArthur in Washington and the Philippines. In November 1942 he commanded the Allied landings in North Africa, and he went on to direct the invasions of Sicily and Italy. Named Supreme Allied Commander in Europe in December 1943, he led the Normandy landings on 6 June 1944 and commanded all Allied forces on the Western Front through the advance into Germany. He was promoted to General of the Army on 20 December 1944, and Germany surrendered unconditionally to the Allies on 7 May 1945.
characters.montgomery: Bernard Montgomery was shot through the lung in the First World War and in 1940 commanded the 3rd Infantry Division in France, briefly leading II Corps at the end of the Dunkirk evacuation. In August 1942 he took over the Eighth Army and won the Second Battle of El Alamein, then led it through Tunisia, Sicily and into Italy. He commanded all Allied ground forces in the Normandy landings and then the 21st Army Group, whose attempt on the Rhine bridges at Arnhem in September 1944 failed. On 4 May 1945 he accepted the surrender of German forces in north-west Europe at Lüneburg Heath.
characters.patton: George S. Patton competed in the modern pentathlon at the 1912 Olympics and led American tanks in the First World War, where he was wounded. In November 1942 he commanded the landing at Casablanca, then restored the shaken II Corps in Tunisia and led the Seventh Army in Sicily, reaching Messina first; there he slapped two shell-shocked soldiers and was removed from battlefield command. He was used as a decoy in the deception plan before D-Day. From 1 August 1944 his Third Army drove rapidly across France, relieved Bastogne during the Battle of the Bulge and advanced deep into Germany.
characters.zhukov: Georgy Zhukov, a peasant's son conscripted into the Tsar's army, defeated the Japanese at Khalkhin Gol in 1939 and became Chief of the General Staff in February 1941. He lost that post after disagreeing with Stalin over Kiev, but took command at Leningrad in September 1941 and then helped direct the defence of Moscow. Made deputy supreme commander in August 1942, he planned the Stalingrad counteroffensive with Aleksandr Vasilevsky and became a Marshal of the Soviet Union in January 1943. In 1945 his 1st Belorussian Front drove from the Vistula to Berlin, and he accepted Germany's surrender there in May.
characters.macarthur: Douglas MacArthur graduated first in his class at West Point in 1903, was highly decorated in the First World War and served as Chief of Staff of the US Army from 1930 to 1935. Recalled in 1941 to command US forces in the Far East, he was forced out of the Philippines by the Japanese invasion and escaped to Australia in March 1942, promising to return. As Supreme Commander, Southwest Pacific Area, he directed the New Guinea campaign and in October 1944 began the liberation of the Philippines. On 2 September 1945 he accepted the formal Japanese surrender aboard USS Missouri.
characters.nimitz: Chester Nimitz, born in Fredericksburg, Texas, was the US Navy's leading authority on submarines and developed the refuelling of ships under way that later let the fleet operate far from port. Chosen to command the Pacific Fleet ten days after Pearl Harbor, he became Commander in Chief, Pacific Ocean Areas, with control of all Allied forces there. Using intelligence from broken Japanese codes, he concentrated his forces to win at Midway in June 1942, then drove across the central Pacific through the Gilbert, Marshall and Mariana Islands. Promoted to fleet admiral in December 1944, he signed for the United States at Japan's surrender on 2 September 1945.
characters.halsey: William Halsey graduated from the Naval Academy in 1904 and took a course in naval aviation before commanding the carrier Saratoga in 1935. Early in the Pacific war he led carrier raids from USS Enterprise on the Gilbert and Marshall Islands and Wake, and commanded the force that launched the Doolittle Raid on Tokyo in April 1942. Given command of the South Pacific Area in October 1942, he directed the Guadalcanal campaign and the advance up the Solomons. Commanding the Third Fleet from 1944, he took his whole fleet north after a Japanese carrier force during the Battle of Leyte Gulf, and that December sailed it into Typhoon Cobra.
characters.cunningham: Andrew Cunningham, known as ABC, was awarded the Distinguished Service Order three times as a destroyer captain. As Commander-in-Chief, Mediterranean Fleet, from June 1939, he sent carrier aircraft against the Italian fleet at Taranto in November 1940, the first all-aircraft naval attack in history, and defeated the Italian navy at Cape Matapan in March 1941. His ships evacuated some 16,500 of the 22,000 men on Crete that May at the cost of three cruisers and six destroyers. He commanded the naval forces for the North African landings in 1942, and in October 1943 became First Sea Lord.
characters.alanbrooke: Alan Brooke, an artillery officer and former commandant of the School of Artillery at Larkhill, commanded II Corps of the British Expeditionary Force in France in 1940 and handled it with distinction in the retreat to Dunkirk. In July 1940 he became Commander-in-Chief, Home Forces, in charge of preparations against invasion. In December 1941 he succeeded Sir John Dill as Chief of the Imperial General Staff, and from March 1942 chaired the Chiefs of Staff Committee, making him Churchill's principal military adviser. He pressed for clearing North Africa and knocking Italy out of the war before the invasion of France, and was promoted to field marshal on 1 January 1944.
characters.dowding: Hugh Dowding, a Scots-born artillery officer, joined the Royal Flying Corps in the First World War and commanded No. 16 Squadron. Before the war he brought the Hurricane and Spitfire into service, and in July 1936 he became the first head of RAF Fighter Command. He built an integrated air defence network of radar, observers, raid plotting and radio control of fighters, known as the Dowding system. In the Battle of Britain in 1940 his command defeated the Luftwaffe's attempt to prepare the way for invasion, but critics of his tactics and of weak night defences in the Blitz had him replaced that November.
characters.mountbatten: Louis Mountbatten, born Prince Louis of Battenberg and a great-grandson of Queen Victoria, began the war commanding the 5th Destroyer Flotilla from HMS Kelly, which was sunk by German dive bombers off Crete in May 1941. As Chief of Combined Operations from October 1941 he oversaw the Bruneval and St Nazaire raids and the disastrous Dieppe Raid of August 1942. In August 1943 Churchill appointed him Supreme Allied Commander, South East Asia Command, whose forces under William Slim retook Burma. On 12 September 1945 he received the formal surrender of the Japanese forces in the region at Singapore.
characters.slim: William Slim was badly wounded at Gallipoli and made his career in the Indian Army. Early in the Second World War he was wounded again in Eritrea, then led the 10th Indian Infantry Division in Iraq, Syria and Persia in 1941. In March 1942 he took command of Burma Corps during the retreat from Burma. As commander of the new Fourteenth Army, drawn mostly from India and Africa, he defeated the Japanese invasion of India at Imphal and Kohima in 1944, supplying surrounded troops by air, and in 1945 took Meiktila and Mandalay before pressing on to recapture Rangoon.
characters.bradley: Omar Bradley graduated from West Point in 1915 in the same class as Eisenhower, and in 1941 commanded the Army Infantry School. His first front-line command came in North Africa under Patton, whom he succeeded at the head of II Corps for the end of the Tunisian campaign and the invasion of Sicily. He commanded the First Army in the Normandy landings of June 1944 and, after the breakout, took over the Twelfth Army Group. With 43 divisions and some 1.3 million men, it became the largest body of American soldiers ever to serve under a single field commander.
characters.konev: Ivan Konev, a peasant's son conscripted into the Tsar's army in 1916, joined the Bolsheviks in 1919 and graduated from the Frunze Military Academy in 1926. He commanded the Kalinin Front from October 1941 in the defence of Moscow and the winter counteroffensive, and led the Steppe Front in the Soviet counteroffensive at Kursk in 1943. His 2nd Ukrainian Front helped trap German forces in the Korsun-Cherkassy pocket early in 1944, and he was made a Marshal of the Soviet Union that February. In 1945 his 1st Ukrainian Front took Kraków, joined the assault on Berlin, met American troops at Torgau on 25 April and entered Prague on 9 May.
characters.donovan: William Donovan commanded the 165th Infantry, the old Fighting 69th, in the First World War and received the Medal of Honor for his actions at Landres-et-Saint-Georges in October 1918. A lawyer and former senior Justice Department official, he travelled to Britain in 1940 and 1941 as an informal envoy, meeting Churchill and the heads of British intelligence. In July 1941 Roosevelt named him Coordinator of Information, and in 1942 the office became the Office of Strategic Services under the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Under his leadership the OSS carried out espionage and sabotage in Europe and Asia, and he rose to major general in November 1944.
characters.turing: Alan Turing, a Cambridge mathematician, described a theoretical computing machine in his 1936 paper On Computable Numbers and earned a doctorate at Princeton in 1938. At the Government Code and Cypher School at Bletchley Park he specified the bombe, an electromechanical machine that searched for Enigma settings more effectively than the Polish bomba it improved upon. As head of Hut 8 he attacked the German naval Enigma, and the resulting intelligence, known as Ultra, helped the Allies in the Battle of the Atlantic. In November 1942 he worked with US Navy codebreakers in Washington, and late in the war he designed a portable secure speech device called Delilah.
characters.oppenheimer: J. Robert Oppenheimer studied at Harvard, took his doctorate at Göttingen under Max Born in 1927, and became a full professor of physics at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1936. His work included the Born-Oppenheimer approximation and early theory of neutron stars and black holes. Recruited to the Manhattan Project in 1942, he became director of its Los Alamos Laboratory in New Mexico in 1943, charged with developing the first nuclear weapons. He was present at the first test of an atomic bomb, Trinity, on 16 July 1945, and in August bombs developed at Los Alamos were used against Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
characters.stilwell: Joseph Stilwell, known as Vinegar Joe for his caustic manner, was sent to China in 1942 as chief of staff to Chiang Kai-shek and commander of US forces in the China Burma India theatre. When the Japanese conquered Burma in 1942 he led a column out on foot, and he later became deputy to Mountbatten at South East Asia Command. His 1944 offensive in northern Burma captured Myitkyina at heavy cost, while the Ledo Road was built to reopen a land route to China. Constant disputes with Chiang led Roosevelt to recall him in October 1944, and in June 1945 he took command of the Tenth Army on Okinawa.
characters.leclerc: Philippe de Hauteclocque, a Saint-Cyr graduate and cavalry officer, escaped German hands after the fall of France in 1940 and joined de Gaulle, taking the name Leclerc to protect his family. In Africa he secured Cameroon for the Free French, helped take Vichy-held Gabon, and raided Italian Libya from Chad. After capturing the oasis of Kufra in early 1941 he had his men swear to fight on until the French flag flew over Strasbourg Cathedral. His 2nd Armoured Division fought in Normandy, led the liberation of Paris in August 1944 and reached Strasbourg that November, and he represented France at Japan's surrender in Tokyo Bay on 2 September 1945.
characters.model: Walter Model made his name in 1942 by holding the Rzhev salient with the Ninth Army against a year of Soviet offensives, and led the northern assault on Kursk in July 1943. Promoted field marshal in 1944, he was sent repeatedly by Hitler to restore collapsing fronts, including Army Group Centre after the Soviet summer offensive. In his retreats he ordered scorched-earth measures, destroying villages and harvests and deporting hundreds of thousands of civilians. Commanding Army Group B in the West, he defeated the Allied airborne landing at Arnhem in September 1944, and took his own life on 21 April 1945 after his forces were trapped in the Ruhr Pocket.
characters.rundstedt: Gerd von Rundstedt, a Prussian officer who had retired as a colonel general in 1938, was recalled for the invasion of Poland in 1939. He commanded Army Group A in France in 1940, and in June 1941 led Army Group South into the Soviet Union, encircling a vast Soviet force at Kiev that September. Hitler relieved him in December 1941 after he allowed a withdrawal from Rostov, but recalled him in 1942 as Commander-in-Chief West. Dismissed after the Normandy landings and reinstated that September, he chaired the military court of honour that expelled officers accused in the July plot so they could be tried and executed.
characters.student: Kurt Student, a First World War fighter pilot, became commander of Germany's first paratroop division in 1938. His paratroopers made the first large-scale airborne assault in history around The Hague on 10 May 1940, and he was shot in the head at Rotterdam. In May 1941 he directed the airborne invasion of Crete, which succeeded at such cost that Hitler forbade further major airborne operations. As temporary commander of Crete, he launched brutal reprisals against the population on Göring's orders, including the massacre at Kondomari and the razing of Kandanos. In 1944 he commanded the First Parachute Army in the West.
characters.galland: Adolf Galland flew ground-attack missions with the Condor Legion in Spain and again in Poland before becoming a fighter pilot in 1940. Flying the Messerschmitt Bf 109, he had 57 victories by the end of 1940 and 96 by November 1941, when he succeeded Werner Mölders as commander of the fighter arm. In early 1942 he planned and commanded the air cover for Operation Cerberus, the Channel Dash of German warships. His clashes with Göring over the air defence of Germany led to his dismissal in January 1945, after which he formed the jet fighter unit Jagdverband 44 and flew with it until the end of the war.
characters.lutjens: Günther Lütjens joined the Imperial German Navy in 1907, served in the First World War, and in the 1930s took the cruiser Karlsruhe around the world on goodwill visits. In April 1940 he had temporary command of the German surface fleet during the landings in Norway, and that summer became Fleet Commander. In early 1941 he led the battleships Scharnhorst and Gneisenau on Operation Berlin, a raid on British shipping in the Atlantic. That May he took the Bismarck and Prinz Eugen into the Atlantic; after Bismarck sank HMS Hood in the Denmark Strait she was hunted down, and he died with most of her crew on 27 May 1941.
characters.ozawa: Jisaburo Ozawa, noted for innovative ideas on the use of aircraft carriers, commanded the Southern Expeditionary Fleet that supported the invasions of Malaya and Thailand in December 1941 and then raided Allied shipping in the Bay of Bengal. In November 1942 he succeeded Nagumo in command of the carrier force, and from March 1944 led the 1st Mobile Fleet. At the Battle of the Philippine Sea in June 1944 his carriers were outmatched by American carrier aviation, and at Leyte Gulf that October his depleted carriers served as a decoy to draw the American fleet north. On 29 May 1945 he became the last commander-in-chief of the Combined Fleet.
characters.homma: Masaharu Homma spent eight years in Britain as a military attaché and served with the British Expeditionary Force in France in 1918, receiving the Military Cross. After commanding a division in China, he was given the 14th Army at the outbreak of the Pacific War and led the invasion of the Philippines. The American and Filipino defenders held Bataan until April 1942 and Corregidor until May. Some 72,000 to 78,000 prisoners taken on Bataan were then forced on the Bataan Death March, in which thousands died from abuse and killings. Homma was removed from effective command soon after Corregidor fell.
characters.balbo: Italo Balbo organised Fascist blackshirt squads in his home region of Ferrara and was one of the four leaders who organised the March on Rome in 1922. From 1926 he built up the Italian air force, and in 1933 he led a formation of 24 seaplanes from Rome to the Chicago exposition and back. That November he was made Governor-General of Libya, a post that removed him from politics in Rome, and he opposed both the partnership with Nazi Germany and the 1938 racial laws. On 28 June 1940, less than three weeks after Italy entered the war, his aircraft was shot down over Tobruk by Italian anti-aircraft guns.
characters.messe: Giovanni Messe trained and led elite Arditi assault troops in the First World War and later served as aide-de-camp to King Victor Emmanuel III. After commanding a corps against Greece, he led the Italian Expeditionary Corps in Russia from 1941, a force he judged poorly equipped for the conditions, until he was replaced in 1942. In February 1943 he took command of the 1st Italian Army in Tunisia and fought a defensive campaign until he surrendered in May 1943, just after being made a Marshal of Italy. After the armistice he became chief of staff of the Italian Co-Belligerent Army fighting alongside the Allies.
characters.kurusu: Saburo Kurusu entered the Japanese diplomatic service in 1910 and spent six years as consul in Chicago, where he married an American, Alice Little. As ambassador to Germany he signed the Tripartite Pact with Germany and Italy in Berlin on 27 September 1940. In November 1941 he was sent to Washington as special envoy to join Ambassador Kichisaburo Nomura in talks with Secretary of State Cordell Hull. On 7 December 1941 the two envoys delivered Japan's note breaking off negotiations after the attack on Pearl Harbor had begun; they were interned and then exchanged in June 1942.
characters.marshall: George C. Marshall graduated from the Virginia Military Institute in 1901 and was a key planner of American operations in France in the First World War, including the Meuse-Argonne offensive. Sworn in as Army Chief of Staff on 1 September 1939, the day Germany invaded Poland, he worked with Secretary of War Henry Stimson to organise the largest military expansion in American history and coordinated Allied operations in Europe and the Pacific. Roosevelt kept him in Washington rather than give him command of the invasion of France, and in December 1944 he became the first General of the Army.
characters.king: Ernest King graduated from the Naval Academy in 1901, commanded submarine divisions, and qualified as a naval aviator in 1927 before commanding the carrier Lexington. He took command of the Atlantic Fleet in February 1941. After Pearl Harbor he became Commander in Chief, United States Fleet, and from March 1942 also Chief of Naval Operations, an unprecedented combination of the Navy's two highest posts. On the Joint and Combined Chiefs of Staff he pressed for a Central Pacific offensive and aid to China, and in May 1943 he formed the Tenth Fleet to direct the campaign against the U-boats. He became a fleet admiral in December 1944.
characters.arnold: Henry H. Arnold learned to fly at the Wright brothers' school in 1911 and became one of the first military pilots in the world. A protege of Billy Mitchell, he became Chief of the Air Corps in 1938 and commanded the US Army Air Forces from their creation in June 1941, sitting on the Joint and Combined Chiefs of Staff. He oversaw their growth from little more than 20,000 men and 800 first-line combat aircraft into the largest and most powerful air force in the world, pressing the development of the B-29 bomber, jet fighters and radar. He was promoted to General of the Army in December 1944.
characters.harris: Arthur Harris emigrated to Rhodesia at 17, fought with the 1st Rhodesia Regiment early in the First World War, and then joined the Royal Flying Corps. At the start of the Second World War he commanded No. 5 Group, and in February 1942 he became head of RAF Bomber Command, which he led for the rest of the war in carrying out the government's policy of area bombing of German cities. He launched the first thousand-bomber raid, on Cologne, in May 1942, followed by the devastating attacks on Hamburg in 1943, Berlin in 1943 and 1944, and Dresden in February 1945, which killed very large numbers of civilians.
characters.tedder: Arthur Tedder flew as a pilot and squadron commander in the Royal Flying Corps in the First World War. As Air Officer Commanding-in-Chief, RAF Middle East, from June 1941 he directed air operations in the Mediterranean and North Africa, including the evacuation of Crete and Operation Crusader, and built the air force that supported victory at El Alamein; his pattern bombing became known as the Tedder Carpet. In 1943 he led Mediterranean Air Command during the invasions of Sicily and Italy. He served as Deputy Supreme Commander under Eisenhower for the invasion of France from January 1944, and signed the German surrender on Eisenhower's behalf in May 1945.
characters.wavell: Archibald Wavell lost his left eye at the Second Battle of Ypres in 1915, winning the Military Cross. As Commander-in-Chief Middle East from July 1939, he launched Operation Compass in December 1940, in which the Western Desert Force under Richard O'Connor destroyed the Italian Tenth Army and took 130,000 prisoners, and he also drove the Italians from Eritrea and Ethiopia. After Rommel's offensive and the failure of Operation Battleaxe, Churchill replaced him with Auchinleck in June 1941, and Wavell became Commander-in-Chief, India, briefly leading the ABDA Command in early 1942. He became Viceroy of India in October 1943.
characters.auchinleck: Claude Auchinleck, an Indian Army officer known as the Auk, commanded the Anglo-French ground forces in Norway in May 1940 and then Southern Command in England before becoming Commander-in-Chief, India. In July 1941 he exchanged posts with Wavell to take over the Middle East, and his Operation Crusader relieved Tobruk by the end of 1941. After the defeat at Gazala and the fall of Tobruk in June 1942, he took personal command of the Eighth Army and halted the Axis advance in the First Battle of El Alamein. Replaced in August 1942, he returned as Commander-in-Chief, India, in June 1943, where his supply and training effort supported Slim's Fourteenth Army.
characters.rokossovsky: Konstantin Rokossovsky rose to senior command in the Red Army but was arrested in Stalin's Great Purge in 1937, imprisoned and tortured, and released only in 1940. After the German invasion he fought at Smolensk and led the 16th Army in the defence of Moscow. His Don Front destroyed the German forces encircled at Stalingrad in early 1943, and that summer his Central Front held the northern face of the Kursk salient. He helped plan and carry out Operation Bagration in 1944, reaching the Vistula opposite Warsaw, was made a Marshal of the Soviet Union that June, and led the 2nd Belorussian Front into Germany in 1945.
characters.vasilevsky: Aleksandr Vasilevsky, a former captain in the Tsar's army, became deputy chief of operations of the Red Army in 1939 and succeeded his mentor Boris Shaposhnikov as Chief of the General Staff in June 1942. Working closely with Georgy Zhukov, he planned the Stalingrad counteroffensive and coordinated the fronts that carried it out, and was made a Marshal of the Soviet Union in February 1943. He helped plan the Battle of Kursk and Operation Bagration, and in February 1945 took command of the 3rd Belorussian Front, taking Königsberg. After Germany's surrender he commanded Soviet forces in the Far East and carried out the invasion of Manchuria in August 1945.
characters.chuikov: Vasily Chuikov, a peasant's son who worked in a factory from the age of 12, joined the Red Army after the revolution and later served as military attaché in China. He commanded the 4th Army in the invasion of Poland in 1939 and the 9th Army in the Winter War against Finland. Given the 62nd Army at Stalingrad in September 1942, he held the ruined city by keeping his front line as close to the Germans as possible until the counteroffensive trapped the German Sixth Army. His army, renamed the 8th Guards, fought through Poland to Berlin, where he accepted the surrender of the city's garrison on 2 May 1945.
characters.spruance: Raymond Spruance commanded a cruiser division in the opening months of the Pacific war and, on Halsey's recommendation, was given Task Force 16, with the carriers Enterprise and Hornet, for the Battle of Midway in June 1942. There American dive bombers sank four Japanese fleet carriers, the turning point of the Pacific war. He then became chief of staff and deputy to Nimitz, and from August 1943 commanded the Central Pacific Force, later the Fifth Fleet, in the capture of the Marshall and Mariana Islands. He commanded at the Battle of the Philippine Sea in June 1944 and in the campaigns for Iwo Jima and Okinawa in 1945.
characters.clark: Mark Clark was seriously wounded as a young captain in France in 1918 and was later noticed by George C. Marshall. He headed the planning for Operation Torch, the Allied landings in North Africa in November 1942, and served as deputy commander of Allied Force Headquarters. As commander of the US Fifth Army from January 1943 he led the landings at Salerno that September, where he won the Distinguished Service Cross, and the hard campaign north through Italy, capturing Rome in June 1944. In December 1944 he took command of the 15th Army Group, and in March 1945 he became a four-star general at 48.
characters.juin: Alphonse Juin, a Saint-Cyr graduate who lost the use of his right arm to a wound in 1915, spent much of his career in North Africa. Captured in the Lille pocket in 1940, he was released in 1941 at Vichy's request and given command of French forces in North Africa. After the Allied landings of November 1942 he joined the Allies and ordered French troops in Tunisia to fight the Axis. His French Expeditionary Corps broke the Gustav Line in Italy in 1944 through its skill in mountain warfare, though its North African troops committed mass rapes of Italian civilians, which he took severe measures to curb.
characters.wingate: Orde Wingate, a Royal Artillery officer and fervent Christian Zionist, formed the Special Night Squads of British soldiers and Jewish volunteers in Palestine in 1938. In 1941 he created Gideon Force, a small British, Sudanese and Ethiopian force that harassed Italian forts and supply lines during the liberation of Ethiopia. In Burma he led the Chindits, long-range columns operating behind Japanese lines, first in February 1943 and again in March 1944, when much of his force was landed by glider. He was killed on 24 March 1944 when his aircraft crashed in the hills of Manipur in north-east India.
characters.chennault: Claire Chennault was an outspoken advocate of fighter aircraft in the US Army Air Corps before retiring as a major in 1937 and going to China, where he became Chiang Kai-shek's chief air adviser. From 1941 he commanded the American Volunteer Group, the Flying Tigers, which fought the Japanese from bases in Burma and China for seven months after Pearl Harbor. When the group was taken into the US Army Air Forces in 1942 he returned to American service, rising to major general in command of the Fourteenth Air Force in China. He quarrelled constantly with General Stilwell and helped persuade Roosevelt to recall him in 1944.
characters.zhu_de: Zhu De, a graduate of the Yunnan Military Academy, fought in the 1911 Revolution and later commanded warlord forces before joining the Chinese Communist Party while in Germany in the 1920s. After helping to organise the Nanchang uprising of 1927, he joined Mao Zedong in the Jinggang Mountains in 1928, where their combined forces became the core of the Red Army, and he took part in the Long March. During the war against Japan he was commander-in-chief of the Communist forces, including the Eighth Route Army, and in 1940 organised the Hundred Regiments Offensive with Peng Dehuai.
characters.menzies: Stewart Menzies, educated at Eton, served with the Life Guards in the First World War, winning the Distinguished Service Order in 1914 before a gas attack in 1915 ended his front-line service. He moved into intelligence at Haig's headquarters and joined the Secret Intelligence Service after the war, becoming deputy to its chief, Admiral Hugh Sinclair. On Sinclair's death in 1939 he became Chief of SIS, and he insisted on wartime control of the codebreakers at Bletchley Park. He personally supplied Churchill with the Ultra decrypts of German Enigma traffic, which proved vital in the Battle of the Atlantic and the Normandy campaign.
